modules.title: 1. Account Setup and Initial Configuration
modules.content:
## Getting Started: Why the First Ticket Matters  

Imagine you’ve just launched your online boutique, **Luna Loom**, and the first customer writes:

> *“I love the dress I ordered, but the size is a bit tight. Can I exchange it?”*

That email is the moment you’ll know whether your support process is ready for real‑world demand. If the message lands in a cluttered inbox, gets lost, or you can’t respond quickly, that delighted shopper may never return. Setting up a **Zendesk** account correctly from day one turns that single email into a tracked, visible **ticket**—the foundation of every organized support interaction.

This chapter walks you through every step needed to get that first ticket into Zendesk, from signing up for a trial or paid account to configuring your company’s profile, branding, timezone, and default support email address. By the end, you’ll have a live Zendesk instance that can receive, display, and respond to customer inquiries, ready for the next steps in the learning path.

---

## 1. Creating Your Zendesk Account  

### 1.1 Choose Between a Trial and a Paid Subscription  

| Option | What You Get | When It’s Best For |
|--------|--------------|--------------------|
| **Free Trial (30 days)** | Full access to the selected plan’s features, no credit‑card required | Exploring the platform, short‑term projects, or proof‑of‑concept |
| **Paid Subscription** | Ongoing access, billing on a monthly or annual basis | Established businesses, long‑term support, or when you need guaranteed uptime |

> **Tip:** Even if you intend to pay later, start with the free trial. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time without losing data.

### 1.2 Step‑by‑Step Account Creation  

1. **Visit the Zendesk Sign‑up Page**  
   - URL: `https://www.zendesk.com/register/`  
   - Select **“Start free trial”** or **“Buy now”** depending on your choice.

2. **Enter Basic Information**  
   - **Name** – Your personal or company contact name.  
   - **Work email** – Must be a valid address you can access (used for verification).  
   - **Phone number** – Optional, but useful for account recovery.

3. **Pick a Subdomain**  
   - Zendesk creates a unique subdomain in the form `yourcompany.zendesk.com`.  
   - Choose something short, memorable, and aligned with your brand (e.g., `lunaloomboutique.zendesk.com`).

4. **Select a Support Plan**  
   - You’ll see the plan options (see Section 2). Choose one now or skip and decide later; you can always change it from the **Admin** console.

5. **Agree to Terms & Submit**  
   - Review the **Terms of Service** and **Privacy Policy**. Tick the box and click **“Create account.”**

6. **Email Verification**  
   - Zendesk sends a verification link to the email you entered.  
   - Open the email, click **“Verify my email”**, and you’ll be redirected to the Zendesk dashboard.

> **What If the Email Doesn’t Arrive?**  
> - Check your spam/junk folder.  
> - Ensure you typed the address correctly.  
> - If still missing, use the **“Resend verification”** link on the login page.

---

## 2. Selecting the Right Support Plan  

Zendesk offers several plans, each adding layers of functionality. Below is a simplified overview (prices are illustrative; check Zendesk’s website for current rates).

| Plan | Core Features | Typical Use‑Case |
|------|---------------|------------------|
| **Essential** | Ticketing, email channel, basic reporting | Small teams (1‑5 agents) handling low volume |
| **Team** | All Essential features + collaboration tools, SLA (Service Level Agreement) management | Growing teams (5‑15 agents) needing response‑time guarantees |
| **Professional** | Adds custom ticket fields, advanced automations, multi‑channel (chat, social) | Mid‑size businesses (15‑50 agents) with diverse support channels |
| **Enterprise** | Full suite – AI‑powered bots, advanced analytics, custom roles | Large organizations (>50 agents) with complex workflows |

### 2.1 Matching Plan Features to Business Needs  

1. **Ticket Volume** – Estimate how many tickets you expect per month.  
   - < 500 tickets → Essential or Team.  
   - 500‑5,000 tickets → Professional.  
   - > 5,000 tickets → Enterprise.

2. **Channel Mix** – If you plan to support **chat, phone, or social media** soon, choose a plan that already includes those channels (Professional or Enterprise). You can add channels later, but starting with the right plan saves migration effort.

3. **SLA Requirements** – Do you need to promise a **“first response within 2 hours”**? SLA management is only available from the **Team** plan upward.

4. **Customization** – Custom ticket fields, branding, and role‑based permissions become essential as your support operation scales. These are part of Professional and Enterprise.

5. **Budget Constraints** – If you’re a startup with tight cash flow, start with **Essential** and upgrade as revenue grows.

### 2.2 Changing Plans Later  

- **Upgrade** – From the **Admin > Subscription** page, click **“Change plan.”** Follow the prompts; the change is effective immediately.  
- **Downgrade** – Allowed only after the current billing cycle ends. Zendesk will retain your data, but features not supported by the lower plan become inactive.

> **Pro Tip:** Keep a spreadsheet of your projected ticket volume and support channel usage for the next 12 months. Review it quarterly and adjust your plan before the next billing cycle.

---

## 3. Configuring Your Company Profile  

A well‑filled company profile makes your Zendesk instance feel like an extension of your brand.

### 3.1 Accessing the Profile Settings  

1. Click the **gear icon** (Admin) in the left sidebar.  
2. Under **“Account”**, select **“Account Settings.”**  
3. You’ll see tabs for **General**, **Branding**, **Localization**, and **Security**.

### 3.2 General Information  

| Field | What to Enter | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Company name** | Full legal name (e.g., *Luna Loom Boutique LLC*) | Appears in ticket notifications and Help Center. |
| **Domain** | Your public website domain (e.g., `lunaloomboutique.com`) | Used for email routing and branding. |
| **Support email** | Default address (e.g., `support@lunaloomboutique.com`) – set up later in Section 4. | Central point of contact for customers. |
| **Phone number** | Optional, for admin alerts. | Helps with account recovery or two‑factor authentication. |

### 3.3 Branding  

1. **Logo** – Upload a PNG or SVG (max 300 KB). This appears in the header of the Help Center and in email footers.  
2. **Primary color** – Choose a hex code that matches your brand (e.g., `#4A90E2`). Zendesk uses this color for button accents and ticket status tags.  
3. **Favicon** – Small icon displayed in browser tabs. Upload a 16 × 16 px image.

> **Best Practice:** Use the same logo and color scheme you use on your website. Consistency reinforces brand trust.

### 3.4 Localization (Timezone & Language)  

1. **Timezone** – Select the region where your support team operates (e.g., **“America/New_York – Eastern Time (US & Canada)”**). All timestamps on tickets and reports will use this timezone.  
2. **Default language** – Choose the language for Zendesk’s UI and system notifications (e.g., **English (US)**). You can enable additional languages later for multilingual support.

> **Note:** Changing the timezone after tickets have been created does **not** alter the original timestamps; it only affects how new timestamps are displayed.

---

## 4. Setting Up the Default Support Email Address  

The email address you give customers (e.g., `support@lunaloomboutique.com`) is the gateway for tickets to enter Zendesk.

### 4.1 Create the Email Alias  

1. **Log in to your domain’s email provider** (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, etc.).  
2. **Create a new mailbox or alias** named **support**.  
   - If you use an alias, forward all incoming mail to a real mailbox that you control.  
   - Ensure the mailbox can receive **HTML** messages (most modern providers do).

### 4.2 Configure DNS Records (Optional but Recommended)  

To improve deliverability and prevent tickets from being marked as spam, add the following DNS records for your domain:

| Record Type | Name | Value | Purpose |
|-------------|------|-------|---------|
| **SPF** | `@` (or your domain) | `v=spf1 include:mail.zendesk.com ~all` | Authorizes Zendesk to send email on your behalf. |
| **DKIM** | `zendesk._domainkey` | Provided by Zendesk (a long string) | Cryptographically signs outgoing mail, proving it’s authentic. |
| **DMARC** | `_dmarc` | `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:postmaster@yourdomain.com` | Gives you visibility into spoofing attempts. |

> **How to Add Records:**  
> - In your domain registrar’s DNS management console, click **“Add Record.”**  
> - Choose the correct type (TXT for SPF & DMARC, CNAME for DKIM).  
> - Paste the values exactly as shown. Propagation can take up to 48 hours, but most changes appear within a few minutes.

### 4.3 Connect the Email to Zendesk  

1. In Zendesk, go to **Admin > Channels > Email**.  
2. Click **“Add address”** and type **support@lunaloomboutique.com**.  
3. Choose **“Forwarding”** (recommended) or **“Direct”**:
   - **Forwarding** – You forward incoming mail from your provider to a unique Zendesk address (e.g., `support@lunaloomboutique.zendesk.com`). This method keeps the original mailbox active for internal use.  
   - **Direct** – Zendesk fetches mail via POP/IMAP; more complex and usually unnecessary for beginners.

4. **Verify Ownership** – Zendesk sends a verification email to the address you entered. Open the email (from `support@lunaloomboutique.com`) and click the verification link.

5. **Set as Default** – In the same **Email** settings page, click the three‑dot menu next to the address and select **“Set as default support address.”** This makes the address the primary source for all new tickets.

### 4.4 Test the Email Integration  

1. From a personal email account, send a message to `support@lunaloomboutique.com` with the subject **“Test ticket – please ignore.”**  
2. Log in to Zendesk, navigate to the **Views** section, and look for the **“Unassigned”** or **“All Unsolved Tickets”** view.  
3. The email you just sent should appear as a new ticket, with the subject line and body intact.

> **If the ticket doesn’t appear:**  
> - Confirm the forwarding rule is active and points to the correct Zendesk address.  
> - Check the **Email Logs** in Zendesk (Admin > Channels > Email > Logs) for any error messages.  
> - Verify DNS records if you receive a bounce or spam notice.

---

## 5. Creating and Managing Your First Ticket  

Now that the support email is live, let’s walk through the full ticket lifecycle—from arrival to resolution.

### 5.1 Ticket Creation Flow  

1. **Customer sends email** → Zendesk receives it via the configured address.  
2. **Zendesk parses the email** → Generates a ticket with:
   - **Subject** (email subject line)  
   - **Description** (email body)  
   - **Requester** (customer’s email address)  
   - **Status** set to **“New.”**  

3. **Ticket appears in the “Unassigned” view** (or any view you configure later).  

### 5.2 Responding to the Ticket  

1. Click the ticket to open the **Ticket Viewer**.  
2. In the **Comment** field, type your reply (e.g., “Hi Emily, thanks for reaching out! We can exchange the dress for a size M at no extra charge. Please let us know your preferred address.”).  
3. **Choose “Public”** to send the response to the customer, or “Private” for internal notes.  
4. Click **“Submit”**. Zendesk automatically sends the reply to the customer’s email address, preserving the ticket thread.

### 5.3 Updating Ticket Status  

- **New → Open** – Happens automatically when an agent (you) first responds.  
- **Open → Pending** – Use when you’ve asked the customer for more information.  
- **Pending → Solved** – Mark as solved once the issue is resolved.  
- **Solved → Closed** – After a configurable period (default 30 days), tickets auto‑close; you can also close manually.

> **Best Practice:** Keep the status accurate. It drives reporting, SLA calculations, and workload visibility for the whole team.

### 5.4 Adding Internal Notes  

Sometimes you need to share information with teammates without notifying the customer (e.g., “Check inventory for size M”). Use the **“Private”** comment type, which appears only in the ticket’s internal history.

### 5.5 Assigning the Ticket  

If you have multiple agents or groups (covered later), you can assign the ticket to a specific **agent** or **group**:

1. Click the **Assignee** dropdown in the ticket header.  
2. Select the appropriate name.  
3. The ticket moves to the assignee’s **“My Open Tickets”** view.

For now, with a single‑agent setup, you’ll simply keep the ticket **unassigned** or assign it to yourself.

### 5.6 Closing the Loop  

After you set the ticket to **Solved**, you’ll receive a **“Ticket solved”** email notification (if you have email notifications enabled). The customer will also get a copy of the final conversation, confirming that the issue is resolved.

---  

## 6. Quick‑Start Checklist  

| ✅ | Task | How to Verify |
|----|------|----------------|
| 1 | Create Zendesk account (trial or paid) | Logged‑in dashboard appears |
| 2 | Verify email address | Clicked verification link in inbox |
| 3 | Choose a support plan that fits your needs | Plan name shown in **Admin > Subscription** |
| 4 | Fill out company profile (name, logo, color, timezone) | Visible in **Admin > Account Settings** |
| 5 | Set up support email address and DNS records | Ticket appears after sending test email |
| 6 | Send a test email and confirm ticket creation | Ticket shows in **Views > Unassigned** |
| 7 | Reply to the test ticket and see email delivery | Customer receives reply in inbox |
| 8 | Update ticket status to **Solved** | Ticket status changes; solved notification sent |

If any step fails, revisit the corresponding section above or consult Zendesk’s help articles (accessible via the Help Center).

---

## 7. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Problem | Why It Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Email not converting to tickets** | Forwarding rule points to the wrong Zendesk address or verification not completed. | Re‑check the forwarding address and click the verification link again. |
| **Tickets show up with the wrong timezone** | Timezone set to UTC or a different region in **Account Settings**. | Update the timezone to your local business zone (Admin > Account Settings > Localization). |
| **Brand colors not appearing** | Uploaded logo or color code is too large or in an unsupported format. | Use a PNG ≤ 300 KB and a valid hex color (e.g., `#FF5733`). |
| **Spam filters block Zendesk replies** | Missing SPF/DKIM or domain reputation issues. | Add the recommended SPF and DKIM records; monitor DMARC reports. |
| **Unable to change plan later** | Attempting to downgrade before the billing cycle ends. | Wait until the current cycle completes, then downgrade via **Admin > Subscription**. |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Start with a live Zendesk account**—whether a free trial or paid subscription—by creating a subdomain and verifying your email.  
- **Select a plan** that aligns with expected ticket volume, channel mix, SLA needs, and budget; you can upgrade later.  
- **Fill out the company profile**: name, logo, brand colors, and timezone. Consistent branding makes the support experience feel seamless.  
- **Configure a default support email address** (e.g., `support@yourdomain.com`) and, if possible, set up SPF/DKIM/DKIM DNS records to keep messages out of spam folders.  
- **Test the whole flow**: send a test email, verify the ticket appears, reply, and close the ticket. This confirms that customers will see a reliable, end‑to‑end support experience.  

With these foundational steps completed, your Zendesk instance is ready to handle real customer inquiries, and you’re prepared to dive deeper into ticket management, automation, and multichannel support in the upcoming chapters.

modules.content:
## A New Agent’s First Login

Maya just finished her onboarding session. She’s been given a **Free Trial** of Zendesk, her manager has set her up with an **Agent** role, and she’s ready to start helping customers. When she clicks the link in her welcome email and enters her credentials, a clean screen greets her. The question she asks herself is simple: *“Where do I go to see the tickets that need my attention?”*  

The answer lies in the layout of the Zendesk interface. Understanding the placement of the **Dashboard**, **Tickets**, **Views**, and **Reporting** areas—and how to move among them—will turn Maya’s first nervous clicks into confident navigation.

---

## 1. The Zendesk Interface at a Glance  

Zendesk’s web UI is built around two primary navigation components:

| Component | What It Looks Like | Primary Purpose |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **Top navigation bar** | Horizontal strip across the top of the screen, usually dark‑blue or gray. | Global actions (search, notifications, profile, help, and switching between major sections). |
| **Left sidebar** | Vertical column on the left, collapsible in many plans. | Quick access to core objects (Dashboard, Tickets, Views, Reporting, Apps). |

Below the sidebar sits the **main workspace**, where the content of the selected section appears. A thin footer may contain legal links or a “Powered by Zendesk” badge, but it does not affect navigation.

### 1.1. Top Navigation Bar Details  

1. **Search bar** – Type keywords, ticket IDs, or user names to locate items instantly.  
2. **Global notifications** – Bell icon shows recent system alerts (e.g., new tickets, SLA breaches).  
3. **Profile menu** – Click your avatar to reach **My Settings**, **Switch account**, **Log out**, and **Help Center**.  
4. **Product switcher** – In larger organizations, a dropdown lets you jump between Zendesk **Support**, **Chat**, **Talk**, or **Guide** products.

### 1.2. Left Sidebar Sections  

| Icon | Label | Typical Content |
|------|-------|-----------------|
| 🏠 | **Dashboard** | High‑level metrics, recent activity, and customizable widgets. |
| 🎟️ | **Tickets** | List of all tickets, filter bar, bulk actions. |
| 👀 | **Views** | Saved filters (e.g., “Open – High Priority”) that act as personal worklists. |
| 📊 | **Reporting** | Pre‑built and custom reports, analytics charts, export options. |
| ⚙️ | **Admin** (visible only to admins) | Settings for users, groups, channels, automations, etc. |

When Maya clicks **Tickets**, the main workspace loads a table of all tickets she can see, based on her permissions. If she later clicks **Views**, the same workspace swaps to show the list of her saved worklists.

---

## 2. Identifying the Core Areas  

### 2.1. Dashboard – Your “Control Center”  

The **Dashboard** is the first page most users land on after logging in. It provides a snapshot of:

- **Ticket volume** (today, this week, this month)  
- **SLA compliance** (percentage of tickets answered within the promised time)  
- **Agent activity** (how many tickets each agent has closed)  

All widgets are **drag‑and‑drop**, so you can rearrange them to match your daily priorities. For a new agent, the default dashboard often includes:

- **Open tickets** count  
- **Pending tickets** count  
- **Recent satisfaction scores**  

Maya can add a widget for “My tickets awaiting response” to keep her focus narrow.

### 2.2. Tickets – The Heart of Support  

The **Tickets** section is a searchable table that lists every ticket in the system (subject to your role’s permissions). Columns typically include:

- **Ticket ID** – Unique number used in URLs and communications.  
- **Requester** – The end‑user who opened the ticket.  
- **Subject** – Brief description of the issue.  
- **Status** – Open, Pending, Solved, Closed.  
- **Priority** – Low, Normal, High, Urgent.  

You can customize which columns appear via the **Display settings** (gear icon) at the top of the table.

### 2.3. Views – Your Personal Worklists  

**Views** are saved filters that present tickets meeting specific criteria. Think of them as “smart folders.” A typical agent might have:

- **My Open Tickets** – Tickets assigned to the agent that are still open.  
- **High‑Priority Unassigned** – Urgent tickets that no one has claimed yet.  
- **Tickets Awaiting Customer** – Tickets where the last public comment came from the agent, and the status is **Pending**.  

Creating a view involves defining:

1. **Conditions** (e.g., Status = Open, Priority = High)  
2. **Columns** to display (Ticket ID, Subject, Group, etc.)  
3. **Sorting** order (most recent first, highest priority first, etc.)  

Admins can share views with entire groups; agents can create personal views for themselves.

### 2.4. Reporting – Turning Data into Insight  

The **Reporting** area houses both **pre‑built reports** (e.g., “Ticket Solved Times”) and **custom reports** you can build with the **Explore** tool. While agents usually view reports in read‑only mode, admins can design dashboards that surface key performance indicators (KPIs) for the whole support team.

Key report types include:

- **Ticket volume trends** (by channel, by day)  
- **First‑reply time** (how quickly agents answer)  
- **Customer satisfaction (CSAT)** scores  

Reports can be exported as CSV files for deeper analysis or scheduled to be emailed to stakeholders.

---

## 3. Moving Between Sections – The Navigation Workflow  

### 3.1. Using the Sidebar  

1. **Locate the icon** you need (e.g., 🎟️ for Tickets).  
2. **Click** once – the main workspace updates instantly.  
3. **Hover** over an icon to see a tooltip if you’re unsure of its meaning.  

The sidebar can be **collapsed** (arrow at the top) to free screen real estate. Collapsing does not hide the icons; it merely shrinks the labels. Maya can toggle this as she works on a wide monitor.

### 3.2. Switching via the Top Bar  

Some users prefer the **product switcher** in the top bar when they need to jump between Zendesk products:

- Click the **grid icon** (nine squares) → select **Guide** to enter the knowledge‑base authoring environment.  
- Choose **Chat** to open the real‑time conversation console.  

The top bar also offers a **quick‑search** shortcut: type `#12345` to jump directly to ticket 12345, regardless of which section you’re currently viewing.

### 3.3. Keyboard Shortcuts (Power‑User Tip)  

For speed, Zendesk supports a handful of keyboard shortcuts (press `?` anywhere to see the list). The most useful for navigation are:

- `g d` – Go to **Dashboard**  
- `g t` – Go to **Tickets**  
- `g v` – Open **Views** list  
- `g r` – Open **Reporting**  

Maya can practice these shortcuts during low‑traffic periods to build muscle memory.

---

## 4. Role‑Based Views: Agent vs. Admin vs. End‑User  

Zendesk tailors the interface based on the **role** assigned to a user. This is central to maintaining security and relevance.

| Role | Primary Interface Elements | What They Can See | Typical Use Cases |
|------|----------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Agent** | Sidebar (Dashboard, Tickets, Views, Reporting) | All tickets they own or are assigned to; shared views; read‑only reports. | Resolving day‑to‑day customer issues. |
| **Admin** | All Agent elements + **Admin** section (Users, Groups, Channels, Automations, etc.) | Full system configuration, all tickets, all reports, user management. | Setting up workflows, permissions, and integrations. |
| **End‑User** (Customer) | **Help Center** (public knowledge base) and **My Activities** in the portal. | Their own tickets, knowledge articles, community posts. | Submitting requests, checking status, self‑service. |

### 4.1. Visual Differences  

- **Admin** sees a gear icon (⚙️) in the sidebar, which is hidden from agents.  
- **End‑users** never see the left sidebar; instead, they navigate via the **Help Center** UI, which is a separate domain (e.g., `support.company.com`).  
- **Agents** have a **Ticket** button that displays a badge with the number of tickets awaiting their action (e.g., “5”).  

### 4.2. Permissions That Influence Navigation  

- **Ticket access** – Agents can only view tickets that belong to their **Group** or are **assigned** to them. Admins can view *all* tickets.  
- **View creation** – Only agents and admins can create Views; end‑users cannot.  
- **Reporting editing** – Only admins (or users granted the “Report Builder” permission) can edit or create new reports.  

Understanding these boundaries helps Maya avoid “permission denied” errors and know when to request assistance from an admin.

---

## 5. Personalizing the Sidebar – Faster Access to What Matters  

Zendesk allows each user to **customize** their sidebar shortcuts, turning the generic list of icons into a personalized command center.

### 5.1. Adding a Favorite View  

1. Open the **Views** list and locate the view you use most (e.g., *My Open Tickets*).  
2. Click the **star icon** next to the view name.  
3. The star turns gold, and the view appears under a new **Favorites** heading at the top of the sidebar.  

Now Maya can reach her primary worklist with a single click, without scrolling through the entire Views list.

### 5.2. Reordering Sidebar Items  

- Hover over the **section header** (e.g., “Views”) until a **drag handle** (≡) appears.  
- Click and drag the header to a new position (e.g., move **Views** above **Tickets**).  

The order persists across sessions, letting each user arrange the UI to match their workflow.

### 5.3. Adding Custom Shortcuts (Admins Only)  

Admins can create **quick‑access links** to internal tools or external resources:

1. In the **Admin** → **Sidebar** area, click **Add shortcut**.  
2. Provide a **label**, **icon**, and **URL** (e.g., link to a shared Google Sheet).  
3. Choose whether the shortcut is visible to **All agents**, **Specific groups**, or **Only admins**.  

Once added, the shortcut appears alongside native icons. While Maya, as an agent, cannot create these shortcuts herself, she can request an admin to add a link to a frequently used resource (e.g., a “Knowledge Base Search” page).

### 5.4. Collapsing Unused Sections  

If Maya never uses the **Reporting** area, she can collapse it:

- Click the **caret** beside the “Reporting” label.  
- The section shrinks, leaving only the icon visible.  

When she needs a report, she can expand it again. This reduces visual clutter and helps maintain focus.

---

## 6. A Walkthrough: From Dashboard to Ticket Resolution  

To cement the concepts, let’s follow Maya through a typical support cycle.

1. **Login** – Maya lands on the **Dashboard**. She sees a red widget indicating “5 tickets pending your response.”  
2. **Jump to Tickets** – She clicks the 🎟️ icon. The tickets table loads, filtered to “All tickets assigned to me.”  
3. **Switch to a View** – She notices a view named “High‑Priority Unassigned.” She clicks the **star** next to it, turning it into a favorite.  
4. **Open a Ticket** – From the view, she selects ticket **#84231**. The ticket detail pane opens in the main workspace.  
5. **Check Reporting** – Later, she wants to see how her average first‑reply time compares to the team average. She clicks the 📊 icon, then selects the “Agent Performance” report.  
6. **Customize Sidebar** – Impressed by the speed of the new view, she drags the “Views” header above “Tickets” so her favorite view sits at the very top of the sidebar.  

By the end of the day, Maya has navigated four major sections, customized shortcuts, and leveraged role‑based visibility—all without leaving the interface.

---

## 7. Common Navigation Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Remedy |
|---------|--------------|--------|
| “I can’t see the **Admin** icon.” | User is not assigned the **Admin** role. | Request role elevation from your manager or confirm with the account admin. |
| “My view does not show any tickets.” | The view’s filter criteria are too restrictive (e.g., looking for **Status = Solved** when you need **Open**). | Edit the view’s conditions or select a different view. |
| “The dashboard widgets are missing.” | The user’s **Dashboard layout** was reset or the account plan limits widgets. | Re‑add widgets via the **Customize** button or verify plan limits with admin. |
| “Clicking a ticket opens a new tab instead of the same workspace.” | Browser settings force links to open in new tabs. | Adjust browser preferences or check for custom **App** settings that modify link behavior. |

Being aware of these issues helps agents like Maya troubleshoot navigation hiccups without needing to involve support staff.

---

## 8. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet  

- **Top Bar**  
  - `?` – Show keyboard shortcuts.  
  - `g d` – Go to **Dashboard**.  
  - `g t` – Go to **Tickets**.  
  - `g v` – Open **Views**.  
  - `g r` – Open **Reporting**.  

- **Sidebar Customization**  
  - ★ – Favorite a view.  
  - Drag handle (≡) – Reorder sections.  
  - Caret (▾) – Collapse/expand a section.  

- **Role Differences**  
  - **Agent** – Sees Tickets, Views, Reporting (read‑only).  
  - **Admin** – All Agent features + **Admin** panel.  
  - **End‑User** – Only Help Center and personal ticket portal.  

---

## Key Takeaways

- The **top navigation bar** provides global actions, while the **left sidebar** houses core objects: **Dashboard**, **Tickets**, **Views**, and **Reporting**.  
- **Dashboard** offers a high‑level snapshot; **Tickets** displays every ticket you can access; **Views** are personalized worklists; **Reporting** turns data into actionable insights.  
- Navigation is accomplished by clicking icons in the sidebar or using keyboard shortcuts; the top bar also lets you switch between Zendesk products.  
- **Agent**, **Admin**, and **End‑user** roles see different UI elements and permissions, shaping what each can view and edit.  
- You can **customize** the sidebar by favoriting views, reordering sections, adding shortcuts (admins), and collapsing unused areas for a cleaner workspace.  

With these fundamentals, you’re ready to move confidently through Zendesk, focus on the tickets that matter, and lay the groundwork for deeper features explored later in the course.

modules.title: 3. Ticket Basics: Fields, Forms, and Statuses
modules.content:
## A Ticket Walk‑through: From “What’s Wrong?” to “All Set”

Imagine you’ve just opened the Zendesk dashboard after a busy morning. In the **Tickets** list, a fresh entry catches your eye:

- **Subject:** *“My printer keeps jamming after the first page.”*  
- **Requester:** *Jane Doe (jane@acme.com)*  
- **Form:** *Hardware Support*  

Jane is a customer who just called the support line. She’s waiting for a solution, and you need to capture the missing details, assign the ticket to the right technician, and keep everyone (including Jane) informed about what’s happening. This single ticket will travel through a series of **fields**, **forms**, and **statuses** before it lands in the **Closed** state. Mastering each of those elements is the foundation of effective Zendesk support.

Below we break down every piece of that journey, starting with the fields that make up a ticket, moving on to custom fields and ticket forms, and finishing with the lifecycle statuses that guide agents and customers alike.

---

## 1. Standard Ticket Fields – The Core Data You’ll Always See

Zendesk tickets come with a set of **built‑in fields** that appear on every ticket, regardless of the form you use. Think of these as the “minimum résumé” a ticket must carry.

| Field | What It Holds | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Subject** | A concise headline of the request (often the email subject line). | Gives agents a quick glance at the issue. |
| **Description** | The full text of the request – the body of an email, chat transcript, or notes you add. | Contains the details you’ll need to troubleshoot. |
| **Requester** | The user who originated the request (email address, name, and Zendesk profile). | Identifies who to reply to and track satisfaction. |
| **Assignee** | The agent (or **group**) currently responsible for the ticket. | Makes ownership explicit and prevents duplication of effort. |
| **CC (Carbon Copy)** | Additional users who receive ticket updates – often managers or other stakeholders. | Keeps the right people in the loop without adding them as requesters. |
| **Tags** | Free‑form keywords you add (e.g., `printer`, `high_priority`). | Powerful for searching, reporting, and triggering automations later. |

> **Tip:** All of these fields are visible on the ticket view you explored in *Chapter 2 – Navigating the Zendesk Interface*. You can edit the **Subject**, type into the **Description**, and assign the ticket using the **Assignee** dropdown.

### 1.1 The Requester vs. the End‑User

In many support scenarios, the **requester** is not the same person who will ultimately use the product. For example, a corporate IT department might submit a ticket on behalf of an employee. Zendesk tracks the **requester** separately from the **assignee**, allowing you to:

- Send status updates to the requester (the person who opened the ticket).  
- Keep internal notes visible only to agents (via the **Internal Note** type).  

When you first set up your account (see *Chapter 1 – Account Setup and Initial Configuration*), you defined a **Free Trial** and later a **Paid Subscription**. Those steps gave you access to the full ticketing features, including the ability to add custom fields and forms – the next topics on our agenda.

---

## 2. Custom Ticket Fields – Capturing the Details That Matter to You

Standard fields cover the basics, but most support teams need extra data points to resolve issues efficiently. **Custom ticket fields** let you collect exactly the information you require, without cluttering the description.

### 2.1 Types of Custom Fields

| Field Type | Typical Use | Example |
|------------|-------------|---------|
| **Single‑line text** | Short, free‑form answers. | *“Serial Number”* |
| **Multi‑line text** | Longer explanations or steps taken. | *“Troubleshooting Steps Already Performed”* |
| **Dropdown (single select)** | Choose one option from a predefined list. | *“Operating System”* → Windows 10, macOS, Linux |
| **Multi‑select dropdown** | Pick multiple applicable options. | *“Affected Features”* → Printing, Scanning |
| **Numeric** | Numbers only – useful for quantities or IDs. | *“Number of Affected Devices”* |
| **Date** | Calendar dates, often for SLA calculations. | *“Installation Date”* |
| **Checkbox** | Yes/No toggle. | *“Is the device under warranty?”* |

> **Note:** Custom fields are **optional** by default. You can mark them **required** in a ticket form (see the next section) if every request of that type must include the data.

### 2.2 Adding a Custom Field – Step‑by‑Step

1. From the main navigation, click **Admin** (the gear icon) → **Ticket Fields**.  
2. Click **Add field** and select the field type you need.  
3. Fill in the **Title** (what agents will see) and **Description** (help text for requesters).  
4. Choose **Field options** where applicable (e.g., the dropdown list).  
5. Click **Save**.  

Your new field now appears on any ticket form that includes it. Remember, you can later edit or deactivate a field, but **deleting** a field permanently removes its data from all tickets – so use caution.

### 2.3 Real‑World Example: A “Device Issue” Form

Suppose your support team handles both software and hardware requests. For hardware tickets you want to capture:

- **Device Type** (dropdown: Laptop, Desktop, Printer, Router)  
- **Serial Number** (single‑line text)  
- **Warranty Status** (checkbox)  

You would create three custom fields as described above, then attach them to a **Hardware Support** ticket form (next section). When Jane submits her printer‑jamming request, the form will prompt her (or the agent on her behalf) to fill in those fields, giving the technician all the data they need before even opening the device.

---

## 3. Ticket Forms – Tailoring the Ticket Layout to the Request Type

A **ticket form** is a container that groups together the standard fields and any custom fields you’ve defined. Think of it as a **template** that appears when a ticket is created, ensuring agents collect the right data for each request category.

### 3.1 Why Use Multiple Forms?

- **Clarity:** Requesters see only the fields relevant to their issue, reducing confusion.  
- **Efficiency:** Agents receive pre‑populated data, cutting down on back‑and‑forth clarification.  
- **Automation‑Ready:** Triggers, automations, and macros can reference the form name to apply specific logic.

### 3.2 Building a Ticket Form

1. In **Admin**, go to **Ticket Forms**.  
2. Click **Add form** and give it a clear name (e.g., *“Software Bug Report”*).  
3. Drag‑and‑drop the desired **standard fields** and **custom fields** into the form layout.  
4. For each field, you can set it to **required**, **visible**, or **hidden**.  
5. Optionally, assign the form to a **group** (e.g., the *Hardware Team*) so tickets created with that form are automatically routed.  
6. Click **Save**.

> **Tip:** Keep the number of required fields low—only ask for information you truly need to start troubleshooting. Over‑asking can increase ticket‑creation friction and lead to abandoned requests.

### 3.3 Selecting the Right Form at Ticket Creation

When an end‑user submits a request via email, chat, or the **Help Center**, Zendesk automatically applies the **default form** you set in **Admin > Ticket Forms**. For more complex channels (e.g., a web form on your site), you can specify which form to use by adding a hidden field named `ticket_form_id` to the submission payload.

Agents can **change the form** after a ticket is opened if they realize the request belongs to a different category. This flexibility is handy when a request is initially mis‑routed.

### 3.4 Form‑Specific Scenario

Returning to Jane’s printer issue:

1. She clicks **Submit a request** on your Help Center and selects “Hardware Problem” from a dropdown.  
2. The Help Center loads the **Hardware Support** form, showing the custom fields *Device Type*, *Serial Number*, and *Warranty Status*.  
3. Jane fills them out, clicks **Submit**, and a new ticket appears in Zendesk with those fields already populated.  
4. The ticket is automatically assigned to the **Hardware Team** because the form is linked to that group.

Now the technician can see the serial number and warranty status at a glance, dramatically shortening the time to resolution.

---

## 4. Ticket Statuses – Guiding a Ticket Through Its Lifecycle

Every ticket moves through a **status** that tells both agents and requesters where the work stands. Zendesk provides five core statuses. Understanding how and when to transition between them keeps your support pipeline transparent and SLA‑friendly.

### 4.1 The Five Core Statuses

| Status | Meaning | Typical Trigger |
|--------|---------|-----------------|
| **New** | The ticket has just been created and has not yet been opened by an agent. | Automatic on ticket creation. |
| **Open** | An agent is actively working on the ticket. | Agent clicks **Open** or replies to the requester. |
| **Pending** | The ticket is waiting for external input (e.g., a customer reply, a third‑party response). | Agent selects **Pending** and adds a note explaining what’s needed. |
| **Solved** | The issue is resolved; the requester has been notified. | Agent clicks **Solve** after confirming the solution. |
| **Closed** | The ticket is archived and can no longer be reopened. | System automatically closes a **Solved** ticket after a set period (default 30 days) or an agent manually closes it. |

### 4.2 Status Transition Flow

```
New → Open → Pending ↘
                ↘   Solved → Closed
                ↗
          (Agent reopens if needed)
```

- **New → Open** – The moment an agent takes ownership or replies.  
- **Open → Pending** – When you need the requester to act (e.g., “Please provide the serial number”).  
- **Pending → Open** – Once the requester replies, you move the ticket back to **Open**.  
- **Open → Solved** – After you have confirmed the fix works.  
- **Solved → Closed** – Automatically after the configured **ticket‑closure period** or manually if you need to lock it sooner.

### 4.3 Who Can Change a Status?

- **Agents** – Can move a ticket through any status (except they cannot directly set **Closed** unless they have the *Close tickets* permission).  
- **Admins** – Have full control, including overriding any restrictions.  
- **End‑users** – Generally cannot change status, but their replies can trigger automations that move a ticket from **Pending** back to **Open**.

> **Tip:** Status changes are recorded in the ticket’s **audit log** (visible in the ticket’s timeline). This audit trail is useful for compliance and for reviewing SLA performance later.

### 4.4 Practical Walk‑through: Jane’s Ticket Journey

| Step | Action | Status Change | Reason |
|------|--------|---------------|--------|
| 1 | Jane submits the request via the Help Center. | **New** → **Open** (auto‑assigned to Hardware Team) | An agent, Alex, claims the ticket. |
| 2 | Alex asks Jane for the printer’s serial number (field already filled, but she’s unsure). | **Open** → **Pending** | Waiting for Jane’s clarification. |
| 3 | Jane replies with the serial number. | **Pending** → **Open** | Information received; work can resume. |
| 4 | Alex troubleshoots, discovers a firmware bug, and applies a fix. | **Open** → **Solved** | Issue resolved; Alex notifies Jane. |
| 5 | After 30 days with no further reply, Zendesk automatically **Closes** the ticket. | **Solved** → **Closed** | System cleanup per default closure period. |

During each transition, Zendesk automatically logs the status change and any accompanying public or internal notes, preserving a complete history of the ticket’s life.

### 4.5 Customizing Statuses (Advanced)

While the five core statuses cover most scenarios, Zendesk **Enterprise** plans allow you to add **custom statuses** (e.g., *“Escalated”*). For the purpose of this beginner guide, we’ll stick to the default set, which is sufficient for most small‑to‑mid‑size support teams.

---

## 5. Best Practices for Managing Fields, Forms, and Statuses

1. **Start Simple, Then Iterate**  
   - Begin with one ticket form per major request type.  
   - Add custom fields only when you spot a recurring data gap.

2. **Use Clear, Action‑Oriented Labels**  
   - Instead of “Device”, write “Device Type (Laptop, Printer, …)”.  
   - For statuses, rely on the default names; they are already well‑known to agents and customers.

3. **Make Required Fields Truly Required**  
   - If a field can be left blank without breaking the troubleshooting process, keep it optional.  
   - Over‑requiring fields leads to abandoned tickets or inaccurate data.

4. **Leverage Tags for Quick Filtering**  
   - Tags like `high_priority` or `needs_escalation` let you locate tickets fast, and they are later usable in triggers and reports.

5. **Document Field Purpose**  
   - Add a short description to each custom field. This description appears as placeholder/help text when agents or requesters view the form.

6. **Set Up Status‑Based SLA Policies Early**  
   - Although SLA configuration comes later (Chapter 5), aligning statuses with SLA milestones (e.g., “First response time” starts at **New**, “Resolution time” ends at **Solved**) ensures you meet expectations from day one.

7. **Regularly Review Form Usage**  
   - Periodically run a report (once you have access to reporting tools) to see which custom fields are rarely filled. Consider removing or consolidating them to keep forms lean.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Standard fields** (Subject, Description, Requester, Assignee, CC, Tags) provide the essential context for every ticket.  
- **Custom ticket fields** let you capture additional, business‑specific data; choose the appropriate field type and mark fields required only when necessary.  
- **Ticket forms** are templates that combine standard and custom fields; use separate forms for distinct request categories to streamline data entry and routing.  
- **Ticket statuses** (New → Open → Pending → Solved → Closed) map the ticket’s lifecycle; agents move tickets through these states to reflect progress and keep requesters informed.  
- Follow **best‑practice guidelines**—keep forms simple, label fields clearly, use tags wisely, and regularly audit field usage—to maintain a clean, efficient ticketing system.  

With a solid grasp of fields, forms, and statuses, you’re now equipped to design tickets that capture the right information, route them to the right people, and guide them smoothly from creation to resolution. Your next step will be to explore **Users, Groups, and Permissions**, where you’ll learn how to control who sees and edits each of these elements.

modules.title: 4. Users, Groups, and Permissions
modules.content:
## Getting the Right People on the Right Tickets Imagine you’re the support manager at **Luna Loom**, a fast‑growing e‑commerce brand that just launched a new line of sustainable sleepwear. Overnight, the help desk is flooded with three types of requests: * **Customer questions** about sizing and fabric care (end‑users). * **Technical tickets** from the website team about checkout errors (agents in the “Web Ops” group). * **Returns and refunds** that must be approved by the finance department (agents in the “Finance” group). If every ticket lands in a single queue, your agents will waste time sifting through unrelated issues, and sensitive financial data could be exposed to the wrong people. The solution? **Set up users, groups, and role‑based permissions in Zendesk** so each ticket automatically lands where the right people can see and resolve it. Below you’ll learn how to: 1. **Add agents and end‑users**—both one‑by‑one and in bulk. 2. **Organise agents into groups** that reflect skill sets or departments. 3. **Assign roles** (admin, agent, light agent) and understand what each role can do. 4. **Configure permission settings** to control ticket visibility and protect private data. --- ## 1. Adding People to Your Zendesk Account ### 1.1. Manual entry – the “quick‑add” method When you only have a handful of new users, the fastest way is to create them directly from the Zendesk interface. 1. From the **Admin** sidebar (refer to *Navigating the Zendesk Interface*), click **People → Team**. 2. Click **Add user** at the top‑right. 3. Fill in the required fields: * **Name** – Full name as it should appear on tickets. * **Email** – Must be a valid work email; Zendesk will send an invitation. * **Role** – Choose **Agent**, **Light agent**, or **Admin** (see Section 2). 4. Click **Save**. The new user receives an email invitation to set a password and log in. > **Tip:** If you need to add an end‑user (a customer who will submit tickets), select **End‑user** as the role. End‑users cannot log into the agent side of Zendesk but can still receive and reply to ticket notifications. ### 1.2. Bulk import – handling dozens or hundreds at once Most growing companies will eventually need to import many agents or customers. Zendesk provides a CSV import tool that maps columns to user attributes. #### Step‑by‑step bulk import 1. **Prepare the CSV file** * Include a header row with exact field names: `Name, Email, Role, Group`. * For agents, specify the role (`agent`, `admin`, `light_agent`). * For end‑users, use `end_user`. * Optional: add custom fields (e.g., `Department`) if you have them set up. 2. **Navigate to People → Team** and click the **Import** button (usually a small arrow icon). 3. **Upload the CSV** and review the field‑mapping screen. Zendesk will attempt to match column headings automatically; adjust any mismatches. 4. **Run a test import** (use a small sample of 5 rows) to verify that roles and groups are assigned correctly. 5. **Execute the full import**. Zendesk will display a progress bar and a summary report once complete. > **Note:** Bulk‑imported users receive the same invitation email as manually added users. If you prefer to set passwords yourself, enable the “Create users without sending invitations” option (available on paid plans). #### Common pitfalls and how to avoid them | Issue | Why it happens | Fix | |-------|----------------|-----| | **Duplicate emails** | CSV contains the same email twice or the email already exists in Zendesk. | Remove duplicates before import or use the “Update existing users” option. | | **Invalid role values** | Role column contains typos (`agnt` instead of `agent`). | Use the exact role strings listed in Zendesk’s documentation. | | **Group not found** | Group name in CSV does not match any existing group. | Create the group first (see Section 2) or use the group’s numeric ID. | --- ## 2. Organising Agents into Groups ### 2.1. What is a **Group**? A **Group** is a collection of agents who share a common responsibility—such as “Web Ops”, “Finance”, or “Customer Success”. Groups are used to: * Route tickets automatically (via triggers, later covered in Chapter 5). * Control who can view or edit a ticket. * Generate group‑specific performance reports. ### 2.2. Creating your first groups 1. Go to **Admin → People → Groups**. 2. Click **Add group**. 3. Enter a **Name** (e.g., *Web Ops*). 4. (Optional) Add a **Description** to remind agents of the group’s purpose. 5. Click **Save**. Repeat the process for each department or skill set you need. For Luna Loom, you might create: * **Customer Service** – handles general inquiries. * **Web Ops** – resolves technical website issues. * **Finance** – processes refunds and billing disputes. * **Product** – answers questions about materials and design. ### 2.3. Assigning agents to groups When adding an agent (Section 1) you can select a **Default group**. This is the group the agent belongs to by default and where tickets are initially assigned if no other routing rule applies. * To change an agent’s group later, edit the user profile, locate the **Group** field, and select a new group. You can also assign an agent to **multiple groups** (available on most paid plans). In the user profile, use the **Groups** multiselect to add additional groups. This flexibility lets senior agents sit in both “Customer Service” and “Finance” if they handle escalations. ### 2.4. Using groups for ticket routing (preview) Although the detailed mechanics of routing are covered in Chapter 5, it helps to understand the basic principle now: **When a ticket’s “Group” field is set, only agents belonging to that group can see the ticket** (unless broader permissions are granted). This is the foundation of secure, organized support. --- ## 3. Roles: Defining What Users Can Do Zendesk ships with three built‑in roles. Each role bundles a set of **capabilities**—the actions a user can perform in the product. Understanding these roles is essential for both security and workflow efficiency. | Role | Primary purpose | Key capabilities | |------|-----------------|-------------------| | **Admin** | Full‑access manager of the Zendesk instance. | • Create, edit, and delete users, groups, and settings.
• Access all tickets, including those in private groups.
• Manage billing, apps, and integrations. | | **Agent** | Front‑line support staff who work tickets daily. | • View, create, edit, and solve tickets in their groups.
• Use macros, triggers, and automations.
• Access the **Help Center** for internal knowledge base articles. | | **Light agent** | Users who need limited ticket visibility (e.g., sales reps). | • View tickets they are explicitly added to as a **CC** or **Follower**.
• Add private comments to tickets they can see.
• Cannot solve tickets or change ticket status. | ### 3.1. Assigning roles When adding a user (Section 1) you choose the role from a dropdown. To change a role later: 1. Open the user’s profile. 2. Click **Edit**. 3. Select a new role and **Save**. > **Caution:** Only **Admins** can assign or modify the **Admin** role. If you accidentally grant admin rights to a non‑trusted user, they could change security settings or export data. ### 3.2. When to use a **Light agent** * **Sales teams** that need to stay informed about a customer’s support history without being able to close tickets. * **Subject‑matter experts** (SMEs) who provide occasional input on complex tickets but should not manage the ticket lifecycle. By limiting their permissions, you protect ticket integrity while still giving them the visibility they need. ### 3.3. Custom roles (advanced) For organizations that need a finer‑grained permission model, Zendesk offers **custom roles** on Enterprise plans. Custom roles let you toggle individual capabilities (e.g., “Can view private tickets”). Because this chapter targets beginners and core plan users, we’ll not dive into custom roles here, but keep them in mind for future scaling. --- ## 4. Controlling Ticket Access with Permissions ### 4.1. The permission hierarchy Zendesk evaluates permissions in the following order (from most specific to most general): 1. **Ticket‑level restrictions** – private tickets, ticket sharing settings. 2. **Group membership** – an agent can see tickets assigned to any of their groups. 3. **Role capabilities** – agents can view tickets they’re allowed to see based on their role. 4. **Organization visibility** – agents can see tickets belonging to organizations they’re linked to (if the setting is enabled). If any level blocks access, the agent cannot view the ticket. ### 4.2. Private vs. public tickets * **Public tickets** – visible to all agents (subject to group and role restrictions). * **Private tickets** – visible only to agents who belong to the ticket’s group and have the “View private tickets” capability (Admins have this by default). When creating a ticket, agents can toggle the **Private** checkbox. Private tickets are useful for: * Sensitive financial disputes (e.g., refund amounts). * Internal investigations that should not be exposed to the broader support team. ### 4.3. Configuring **Group‑based permissions** By default, any agent in a group can see all tickets assigned to that group. However, you can tighten control: 1. **Admin → Security → Ticket Access**. 2. Enable **“Restrict access to tickets by group”** (available on most paid plans). When this option is on, agents can only view tickets that are explicitly assigned to a group they belong to. This prevents, for example, a **Customer Service** agent from accidentally opening a **Finance** ticket. ### 4.4. Organization‑level visibility If you have **Organizations** set up (covered in Chapter 3), you can enable **“Organization sharing”** so that all agents in the same organization can view each other’s tickets. This is handy when multiple agents need to collaborate on a single customer’s case across departments. To toggle: 1. **Admin → People → Organizations**. 2. Click **Settings** and turn on **“Allow agents to see tickets from other agents in the same organization.”** > **Best practice:** Use organization sharing sparingly. Over‑sharing can dilute the security benefits of group‑based permissions. ### 4.5. Data privacy considerations Zendesk stores personally identifiable information (PII) such as email addresses, phone numbers, and payment details. To stay compliant with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA): * **Limit who can view PII** – assign only the necessary agents (e.g., Finance) to groups that need that data. * **Enable data‑masking** – in **Admin → Security**, you can mask certain fields for agents with lower privileges. * **Audit log** – Admins can review the **Audit log** (under **Admin → Security**) to see who accessed or modified tickets containing sensitive data. --- ## 5. Practical Workflow: From End‑User to Resolved Ticket Putting the pieces together, let’s walk through a typical ticket lifecycle at **Luna Loom**. 1. **A customer submits a return request** via the web form (Ticket Basics covered earlier). 2. The ticket is automatically **assigned to the “Finance” group** by a trigger (Chapter 5). 3. **Finance agents** (role: **Agent**) receive the ticket in their queue. Because the ticket contains payment information, the **Private** flag is set. 4. A **Light agent** from Sales, who is CC’d on the ticket, can view the ticket but **cannot edit** the private fields or change its status. 5. The **Finance admin** (role: **Admin**) reviews the ticket, processes the refund, and marks the ticket **Solved**. 6. The **Customer Service group** receives a copy of the solved ticket for future reference, but because the ticket is private, only agents with the “View private tickets” capability (Admins) can see the payment details. Through this flow, every stakeholder sees exactly what they need—no more, no less. --- ## 6. Tips for Maintaining a Clean User Structure * **Regularly audit groups** – quarterly, review group memberships to ensure agents are still in the correct groups. * **Use naming conventions** – e.g., `Dept – Function` (`Finance – Refunds`) to keep group lists readable. * **Limit admin accounts** – best practice is to have **no more than three** active admins. Use **Admin‑only** accounts for critical configuration changes. * **Document role responsibilities** – maintain a short internal wiki page that outlines what each role can do; this reduces confusion for new hires. * **Leverage bulk import for de‑provisioning** – when an employee leaves, export the current user list, remove the departed user, and re‑import the cleaned CSV to avoid orphaned accounts. --- ## 7. Frequently Asked Questions **Q1. Can an end‑user be added to a group?** *No.* End‑users do not have access to the agent interface, so group membership does not apply to them. They are simply linked to tickets via the requester field. **Q2. What happens if an agent belongs to multiple groups?** The agent sees tickets from **all** of their groups. If a ticket is assigned to any of those groups, it appears in the agent’s queue. **Q3. Is it possible to hide a ticket from a specific agent while still keeping it in their group?** Yes. Use **private tickets** or **ticket sharing** settings to restrict visibility further. Only agents with the appropriate capability (e.g., “View private tickets”) will see the ticket. **Q4. How do I change a user’s email address?** Open the user profile, click **Edit**, modify the email field, and **Save**. The user will receive a new invitation email to verify the change. **Q5. Do Light agents count toward my agent license limit?** Light agents require a separate **Light agent** license, which is typically cheaper than a full agent license. Check your subscription details for exact counts. --- ## Key Takeaways * **Add users** manually for a few individuals or use a CSV **bulk import** for large onboarding batches. * **Groups** cluster agents by skill or department, enabling automatic ticket routing and controlled visibility. * **Roles** determine what actions a user can perform: **Admin** (full control), **Agent** (standard ticket handling), **Light agent** (limited visibility). * **Permission settings**—including private tickets, group‑based access, and organization sharing—ensure that only the right people see sensitive data. * Regular **audits** and clear **naming conventions** keep your support org tidy and secure, laying a solid foundation for scaling your Zendesk operation.

modules.title: 5. Automations, Triggers, and Macros
modules.content:
## Understanding Triggers vs. Automations  

When a ticket lands in Zendesk, you have two primary tools to make the system act on its own: **triggers** and **automations**. Both belong to the *Business Rules* family (see Chapter 2 for where the admin menus live), but they differ in **when** they fire and **how** they are evaluated.  

| Aspect | **Trigger** | **Automation** |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **Timing** | Fires **immediately** after a ticket is created or updated, as soon as the defined conditions are met. | Runs on a **schedule** (e.g., every hour, once a day). It checks tickets that already exist and meet the conditions at that moment. |
| **Typical Use** | Real‑time alerts, routing tickets to the right group, setting priorities, adding tags. | Periodic clean‑ups, SLA escalations, closing stale tickets, sending follow‑up emails. |
| **Performance Impact** | Executed for every matching event; too many complex triggers can slow ticket processing. | Executed less frequently, so they are safe for bulk operations. |
| **Visibility** | Listed under **Admin > Business Rules > Triggers**. | Listed under **Admin > Business Rules > Automations**. |

Think of a trigger as a **fire‑alarm** that rings the moment smoke appears, while an automation is a **night‑time patrol** that walks the floor every hour to spot anything that needs attention.

> **Quick tip:** Keep the number of active triggers low (under 15) and the number of automations moderate (under 10) to maintain a snappy support experience.

---

## Creating a Trigger that Notifies Agents When a High‑Priority Ticket Arrives  

### Scenario  
Your support team receives dozens of tickets each day, but **high‑priority** tickets (e.g., “System Down”) must be acted on within minutes. You want an instant, visible notification for every agent in the “Tier 1” group whenever such a ticket is created.

### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Navigate to Triggers**  
   - From any Zendesk view, click the **gear icon** (Admin) → **Business Rules** → **Triggers**.  

2. **Add a New Trigger**  
   - Click **Add trigger** (top‑right).  

3. **Name and Description**  
   - **Title:** *High‑Priority Ticket Alert*  
   - **Description (optional):** *Notifies Tier 1 agents when a ticket with priority “Urgent” is created.*  

4. **Set Conditions**  
   - **All of the following conditions must be true:**  
     - **Ticket** → **Is** → **Created** (ensures it runs only on new tickets).  
     - **Priority** → **Is** → **Urgent** (or **High**, depending on your priority naming).  
     - **Group** → **Is** → **Tier 1** (optional – limits the trigger to tickets already assigned to that group).  

5. **Define Actions**  
   - **Notify target** → **Agents in group** → **Tier 1**  
     - **Subject:** *🚨 New High‑Priority Ticket: {{ticket.id}}*  
     - **Message:**  
       ```
       A new urgent ticket has been opened.
       • Subject: {{ticket.title}}
       • Requester: {{ticket.requester.name}} ({{ticket.requester.email}})
       • Link: {{ticket.link}}
       Please respond within the SLA.
       ```  
   - **Add tag** → **high_priority_alert** (useful for reporting later).  

6. **Save**  
   - Click **Create**. The trigger is now active.

### Testing the Trigger  

1. Open a fresh ticket (use the “Submit a request” form you saw in Chapter 3).  
2. Set its **Priority** to **Urgent** and assign it to **Tier 1** (or leave unassigned if you omitted the group condition).  
3. Submit.  

All agents in the Tier 1 group should receive an email (or internal notification, depending on their notification settings) within seconds. Verify the tag **high_priority_alert** appears on the ticket.

### Common Pitfalls  

- **Over‑triggering:** If you forget the “Is Created” condition, the trigger will fire on every update, spamming agents.  
- **Missing Notification Settings:** Agents can mute email notifications; remind them to keep **Ticket Updates** turned on in their profile.  

---

## Building an Automation to Close Solved Tickets After a Set Period  

### Scenario  
Your SLA requires that tickets resolved for more than **7 days** be automatically closed to keep the queue tidy. You need a scheduled rule that identifies such tickets and transitions them to the **Closed** status without manual effort.

### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Navigate to Automations**  
   - Admin (gear) → **Business Rules** → **Automations**.  

2. **Add a New Automation**  
   - Click **Add automation**.  

3. **Name and Description**  
   - **Title:** *Auto‑Close Solved Tickets >7 Days*  
   - **Description:** *Closes tickets that have been in the “Solved” status for more than a week.*  

4. **Set Conditions**  
   - **All of the following conditions must be true:**  
     - **Ticket** → **Status** → **Is** → **Solved**  
     - **Ticket** → **Hours since solved** → **Greater than** → **168** (7 days × 24 hours).  
   - **Any of the following conditions (optional):**  
     - **Ticket** → **Group** → **Is not** → **Escalations** (exclude tickets that may need further review).  

5. **Define Actions**  
   - **Status** → **Closed**  
   - **Add tag** → **auto_closed** (helps later reporting).  

6. **Save**  

### How the Automation Works  

- The automation runs **once per hour** (Zendesk’s default schedule).  
- It scans all tickets; any ticket that meets the conditions gets its status changed to **Closed** instantly.  

### Verifying the Automation  

1. Locate a ticket that is **Solved** and has been so for more than 7 days (you can manually edit the **Solved at** date in the ticket’s **Incidents** tab if needed).  
2. Wait up to an hour, then refresh the ticket. It should now show **Closed** and carry the **auto_closed** tag.  

### Tips for Maintenance  

- **Review daily:** Go to **Automations** → **Run history** to see how many tickets were closed each run.  
- **Adjust the threshold:** If agents need more time to verify closure, change the **Hours since solved** value.  

---

## Designing and Using Macros for Common Responses  

### What Is a Macro?  

A **macro** is a predefined set of actions—typically a text response, status change, tag addition, or ticket field update—that you can apply to a ticket with a single click. Think of it as a **canned reply** that also automates routine ticket housekeeping.

### Scenario  

Your team frequently receives password‑reset requests. Instead of typing the same instructions each time, you’ll create a macro that:

1. Inserts the standard password‑reset guide.  
2. Sets the ticket status to **Pending** (awaiting user confirmation).  
3. Adds the tag **password_reset** for reporting.

### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Open the Macro Builder**  
   - Admin (gear) → **Macros** → **Add macro**.  

2. **Name the Macro**  
   - *Password Reset – Send Instructions*  

3. **Add Actions** (click **Add action** for each line):  

   - **Comment/Description** → **Public reply**  
     ```
     Hi {{ticket.requester.name}},

     To reset your password, please follow these steps:
     1. Click the “Forgot password?” link on the login page.
     2. Enter your email address and click “Submit”.
     3. Check your inbox for a reset link (it may take a few minutes).
     4. Follow the link and choose a new password.

     If you run into any issues, reply to this ticket and we’ll help you further.

     Thanks,
     {{current_user.name}}
     ```  
   - **Status** → **Pending**  
   - **Add tag** → **password_reset**  

4. **Save**  

### Applying the Macro  

1. Open any ticket that matches the scenario (e.g., subject contains “reset password”).  
2. In the ticket editor, click the **Macros** icon (lightning bolt).  
3. Select *Password Reset – Send Instructions*.  

The macro instantly inserts the formatted response, updates the status, and tags the ticket.  

### Managing Macros  

- **Organize by groups:** Use the **Group** field in the macro to limit visibility (e.g., only the **Support** group can see certain macros).  
- **Version control:** If you need to tweak wording, edit the macro and **Save as new version** to keep a history.  

### Best Practices  

- **Keep macros concise:** Long macros can overwhelm agents; break complex procedures into multiple macros if needed.  
- **Use placeholders:** `{{ticket.requester.name}}` and `{{current_user.name}}` keep messages personal.  
- **Tag consistently:** Tags like **password_reset** become powerful filters in reports (covered in Chapter 8).  

---

## Putting It All Together: A Sample End‑to‑End Workflow  

1. **Ticket Creation** – A customer submits a “System Down” request via the web form (Chapter 3).  
2. **Trigger Fires** – The *High‑Priority Ticket Alert* trigger sends an immediate notification to Tier 1 agents and tags the ticket.  
3. **Agent Response** – The agent uses the *System Down – Initial Response* macro (pre‑written with troubleshooting steps) to reply instantly, setting the ticket to **Open**.  
4. **Resolution** – After the issue is fixed, the agent marks the ticket **Solved**.  
5. **Automation Runs** – Seven days later, the *Auto‑Close Solved Tickets >7 Days* automation closes the ticket automatically, adding the **auto_closed** tag.  

This flow eliminates manual steps: the urgent alert reaches the right people instantly, the agent’s first reply is one click away, and the ticket is cleared from the queue without forgetting any stale items.

---

## Common Questions and Troubleshooting  

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| **Can a trigger and automation act on the same ticket?** | Yes. Triggers fire on creation/update; automations may later modify the ticket (e.g., close it). Just ensure they don’t conflict (e.g., an automation that re‑opens a ticket a trigger later closes). |
| **What if an agent wants to suppress a trigger notification for a specific ticket?** | Add a **checkbox custom field** called *Suppress alerts* and include it in the trigger’s conditions (`Is not` *Checked*). Agents can toggle it per ticket. |
| **Do macros work on tickets that are already closed?** | No. Closed tickets are read‑only. Use a macro that **Reopens** the ticket first, then apply the desired actions. |
| **How often do automations run?** | By default every hour. You can’t change the schedule, but you can add multiple automations with different conditions to approximate more frequent runs. |
| **Will tags added by triggers be visible in ticket reports?** | Absolutely. Tags are searchable and appear in any report that includes the **Tags** field (Chapter 8 will cover reporting). |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Triggers** act **immediately** when a ticket meets defined conditions; use them for real‑time alerts, routing, and tagging.  
- **Automations** run on a **schedule** (hourly) and are ideal for bulk actions like closing stale tickets.  
- A well‑crafted **trigger**—such as the *High‑Priority Ticket Alert*—ensures urgent issues reach the right agents instantly.  
- An **automation**—like *Auto‑Close Solved Tickets >7 Days*—keeps your ticket backlog clean without manual effort.  
- **Macros** combine canned replies with ticket updates, letting agents respond with a single click while maintaining consistency and adding useful tags.  
- Combining these tools creates streamlined, repeatable workflows that reduce response times, improve data quality, and free agents to focus on complex problems.

modules.title: 6. Building a Help Center and Knowledge Base
modules.content:
## Enabling the Help Center and Picking a Theme  

Imagine you’ve just launched a new feature for your SaaS product. Within the first hour, the support inbox starts filling with the same three questions: *“How do I reset my password?”*, *“Where can I find the API docs?”*, and *“Why isn’t my integration syncing?”*. Each ticket requires the same short answer, and your agents spend a disproportionate amount of time typing identical replies.  

The quickest way to stop the ticket flood is to give customers a place where they can find the answers themselves—a **Help Center** powered by Zendesk Guide. Once the Help Center is live, you can direct users to the relevant article with a single link, freeing agents to focus on more complex issues.

### 1. Turn on Guide  

1. **Navigate to the Guide admin** – From the Zendesk navigation bar (the one you explored in *Navigating the Zendesk Interface*), click the **Products** menu and select **Guide**.  
2. **Start the setup wizard** – If Guide is still disabled, you’ll see a banner prompting you to **Enable Guide**. Click **Get started**.  
3. **Choose a plan** – For most beginners, the **Free** plan is sufficient to launch a basic Help Center. If you need multilingual support or advanced branding, consider the **Professional** or **Enterprise** tiers (you can upgrade later).  
4. **Confirm the subdomain** – The subdomain you selected during *Account Setup* (e.g., `yourcompany.zendesk.com`) will also serve as the URL for the Help Center (`support.yourcompany.com` if you set up a custom domain).  

> **Tip:** The Help Center lives on the same Zendesk instance as your tickets, so all the **Users**, **Groups**, and **Permissions** you defined earlier are instantly available for controlling article access.

### 2. Select a Theme  

A **theme** is the visual template that determines colors, fonts, layout, and responsive behavior of your Help Center. Zendesk ships with several pre‑built themes:

| Theme | When to use it |
|-------|----------------|
| **Classic** | Simple, clean look; good for minimal branding. |
| **Modern** | Bold colors, larger hero images; fits startups that want a splashy front page. |
| **Help Center Starter** | Designed for quick launch; includes ready‑made sections for common support topics. |

1. In Guide, go to **Guide admin > Customize design**.  
2. Click **Change theme** and preview each option.  
3. Select the theme that matches your brand style and click **Apply**.  

If you prefer a completely custom look, the **Theme editor** lets you edit HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. For beginners, we recommend sticking with a built‑in theme and tweaking colors via the **Branding** panel (logo, primary color, accent color).  

---

## Writing and Organizing Articles  

A Help Center is only as useful as its content. The goal is to create **self‑service resources** that are easy to find and understand. Below is a step‑by‑step workflow that mirrors the way you’d create a ticket in Zendesk, but with a focus on knowledge sharing instead of problem resolution.

### 1. Create the First Article  

1. **Open the article editor** – In Guide admin, click **Add article** (top‑right).  
2. **Title** – Use a clear, searchable phrase. *“How to reset your password”* is better than *“Password help”*.  
3. **Body** – The rich‑text editor lets you add headings, lists, images, and videos.  
   - **Use headings** (`<h2>`, `<h3>`) to break steps into logical chunks.  
   - **Add screenshots** by dragging them into the editor; Zendesk automatically hosts the image.  
   - **Include a “Related articles”** section at the bottom to guide users to other relevant content.  
4. **Save as draft** – This keeps the article invisible to the public until you’re ready.  

> **Note:** Because you already know how to **add attachments** to tickets (see *Ticket Basics*), you’ll find the same process here when inserting images.

### 2. Build the Hierarchical Structure  

Zendesk Guide organizes content in a three‑level hierarchy:

1. **Categories** – Top‑level containers (e.g., *Getting Started*, *Account Management*, *Technical Issues*).  
2. **Sections** – Sub‑folders within a category (e.g., under *Technical Issues*: *API*, *Integrations*, *Troubleshooting*).  
3. **Articles** – Individual knowledge pieces.

#### Best‑practice steps  

1. **Sketch a map** – Before you click “Add category,” sketch a quick outline on paper or a whiteboard.  
2. **Create categories** – In Guide admin, click **Add category**. Keep the number to 4‑6; too many top‑level items overwhelm visitors.  
3. **Add sections** – Inside each category, click **Add section**. Aim for 2‑4 sections per category.  
4. **Place articles** – Drag and drop articles into the appropriate section, or select the section while creating the article.  

**Example hierarchy for a SaaS startup**

```
Getting Started
 └─ Account Setup
     ├─ How to create an account
     └─ How to verify your email
Technical Issues
 └─ API
     ├─ Authentication guide
     └─ Rate‑limit FAQ
```

### 3. Writing Tips for Beginners  

- **Answer the “What, Why, How”** in the first paragraph.  
- **Use plain language** – Avoid internal jargon unless you define it.  
- **Keep steps short** – One action per bullet.  
- **Add a “Last updated” date** – Shows the article is maintained.  

---

## Setting Up Article Permissions  

Not every article should be visible to every visitor. Zendesk Guide respects the same **Roles** and **Groups** you configured in *Users, Groups, and Permissions*.

### 1. Permission Levels  

| Permission | Who can see it |
|------------|----------------|
| **Public** | Anyone on the internet (default). |
| **Signed‑in** | Only logged‑in users (any role). |
| **Internal** | Agents only; useful for troubleshooting guides. |
| **Restricted** | Specific groups or organizations (e.g., premium customers). |

### 2. Applying Permissions  

1. Open an article in edit mode.  
2. Click the **Permissions** tab.  
3. Choose one of the four options.  
4. If you select **Restricted**, a dropdown appears where you can pick the groups that have access.  

> **Tip:** Use **Internal** articles for “How to troubleshoot a failed webhook” – this prevents customers from seeing internal processes while still giving agents a quick reference.

### 3. Controlling Access at the Section Level  

Permissions can also be set at the **section** level, cascading down to all articles within. This is handy when you have an entire category meant for **Partner** users only.  

---

## Optimizing Articles for Search Engines (SEO)  

Even the best‑written article is useless if users can’t find it. Zendesk Guide offers built‑in SEO controls that let you influence how search engines rank your pages.

### 1. Edit SEO Settings  

1. While editing an article, click the **SEO** tab.  
2. Fill in the following fields:  

   - **Meta title** – Usually the article title plus your brand (e.g., “Reset your password – Acme Support”).  
   - **Meta description** – A concise 150‑160‑character summary; appears under the title in Google results.  
   - **Slug** – The URL part after the domain (e.g., `reset-password`). Keep it short and keyword‑rich.  

### 2. Keywords and Internal Search  

- **Keyword focus** – Identify the primary phrase users will type (e.g., “reset password”). Use it naturally in the title, headings, and first paragraph.  
- **Internal search** – Guide’s built‑in search uses the same content. Adding **tags** (via the **Add tag** field) helps surface articles when customers type related terms.  

### 3. Robots and Indexing  

For **Internal** or **Restricted** articles, Zendesk automatically adds a `noindex` meta tag, preventing search engines from crawling them. For public articles, you can control indexing by toggling the **Allow search engines to index this article** switch.  

---

## Integrating the Help Center Widget into Your Website  

Now that your knowledge base is live, you need to make it reachable from your product’s website or web app. Zendesk provides two primary ways to embed self‑service access:

1. **Web Widget** – A floating button that opens a modal with the Help Center, chat, and ticket‑submission forms.  
2. **Guide Widget** – A lightweight script that embeds a searchable Help Center panel directly on a page.

For a beginner, the **Web Widget** is the fastest route.
