### 1. Add the Web Widget Script  

1. In Zendesk, go to **Admin > Channels > Widget**.  
2. Copy the JavaScript snippet that looks like:

   ```html
   <script id="ze-snippet" src="https://static.zdassets.com/ekr/snippet.js?key=YOUR_KEY"></script>
   ```

3. Paste the snippet just before the closing `</body>` tag of your website’s HTML template.  

> **Tip:** If you’re using a CMS (WordPress, Shopify, etc.), most have a “Footer Scripts” field where you can drop the snippet without editing code directly.

### 2. Configure the Widget  

Within the same **Widget** admin page, you can customize:

- **Color** – Match your brand’s primary color.  
- **Position** – Bottom‑right is default; you can move it to bottom‑left if it conflicts with other UI elements.  
- **Features** – Turn on/off **Help Center**, **Chat**, **Ticket Form**. For a pure knowledge‑base experience, disable chat and ticket submission.  

### 3. Test the Integration  

- **Open your site** in an incognito window.  
- Click the floating button; the modal should appear with a search bar and a list of your categories.  
- Perform a test search (e.g., “reset password”) and verify the correct article loads.  

If you need a more embedded experience (e.g., a dedicated **Support** page that shows the full Help Center), use the **Guide Widget**:

1. In Guide admin, go to **Customize design > Widgets**.  
2. Enable **Embedded Help Center** and copy the generated `<iframe>` code.  
3. Place the `<iframe>` on the page where you want the full Help Center to appear.  

---

## Publishing, Testing, and Ongoing Maintenance  

### 1. Publish Articles  

- When an article is ready, click **Publish**.  
- Use the **Version history** tab to track changes—useful for compliance or rollback.  

### 2. Perform a User Acceptance Test (UAT)  

1. **Create a test end‑user** (you can use a personal email address).  
2. **Log in** to the Help Center as that user and verify that:  
   - Public articles are visible without login.  
   - Restricted articles appear only after sign‑in.  
   - The SEO meta title appears correctly in the browser tab.  
3. **Check mobile responsiveness** – The built‑in themes are responsive, but confirm that images and tables scale correctly.  

### 3. Set Up a Review Cycle  

- **Monthly audit** – Scan for outdated articles (look for the “Last updated” date).  
- **Feedback loop** – Enable the **Article rating** widget (thumbs up/down) so customers can flag content that needs improvement.  
- **Analytics** – Once you reach *Reporting and Analytics* (later chapter), you’ll see which articles reduce ticket volume the most.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Enable Guide** to launch a Help Center; pick a built‑in theme that aligns with your brand.  
- **Structure content** using categories → sections → articles; keep the hierarchy shallow and intuitive.  
- **Write clear, searchable articles**—answer the “what, why, how” early, use plain language, and add screenshots.  
- **Control visibility** with article permissions (Public, Signed‑in, Internal, Restricted) and leverage the same **Roles** and **Groups** you set up for ticket routing.  
- **Boost discoverability** by filling out SEO fields (meta title, description, slug) and adding relevant tags.  
- **Embed the Help Center** on your website using the Zendesk Web Widget (quickest) or Guide Widget (full‑page).  
- **Publish, test, and maintain** articles regularly; use ratings and future analytics to refine the knowledge base.  

By following these steps, you’ll transform a growing flood of repetitive tickets into a self‑service experience that empowers customers and frees your agents for higher‑value work.

modules.title: 7. Multichannel Support: Email, Chat, Phone, and Social
modules.content:
## Why Multichannel Matters  

Imagine Maya, a customer‑service manager at a fast‑growing e‑commerce brand. Over a single weekend her team receives **200 emails**, **120 live‑chat requests**, **30 phone calls**, and a flurry of **Twitter mentions**. Each channel lives in a different inbox, phone system, or social‑media dashboard, and agents spend precious minutes switching between tools, often missing or duplicating tickets.  

When Maya consolidates every inbound request into **Zendesk**, her agents see **one unified ticket list**, can apply the same **triggers** and **macros** they already use for email, and route each conversation to the right group with a single click. The result? Faster response times, happier customers, and a clearer view of support workload.  

In this chapter you’ll learn how to **connect each support channel**—email, chat, phone, and social—so that all interactions flow into Zendesk tickets you already know how to manage.

---

## Setting Up Email Support  

### 1. Choose Your Email Strategy  

| Option | How it works | When it’s best |
|--------|--------------|----------------|
| **Zendesk‑provided address** (e.g., support@yourcompany.zendesk.com) | Zendesk automatically creates tickets from incoming mail. No forwarding needed. | Small teams, quick start, no custom domain. |
| **Custom support address** (e.g., support@yourcompany.com) | Your existing mailbox forwards messages to Zendesk. Gives brand consistency. | Established brands that already own a support address. |

### 2. Connect a Custom Support Email  

1. **Navigate to** **Admin ▶ Channels ▶ Email**.  
2. Click **Add address** and enter the full email you want Zendesk to monitor (e.g., **support@yourcompany.com**).  
3. Zendesk will display **MX record** and **SPF** values. Add these to your domain’s DNS so mail servers trust Zendesk as a legitimate sender.  
4. Click **Verify**. Once the DNS changes propagate (usually < 24 h), Zendesk will show a green checkmark.

> **Tip:** If you’re unsure how to edit DNS records, your domain registrar’s help center usually has step‑by‑step guides.  

### 3. Set Up Forwarding Rules (if you keep the mailbox in Gmail, Outlook, etc.)  

| Platform | Forwarding steps |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Gmail** | *Settings ▶ Forwarding and POP/IMAP* → **Add a forwarding address** → enter the **Zendesk‑generated address** shown in the previous step → confirm the verification email. |
| **Outlook/Office 365** | *Admin Center ▶ Exchange* → **Mail flow** → **Rules** → **+ Add a rule** → **Apply to all messages** → **Redirect the message to** → paste the Zendesk address. |
| **Other providers** | Look for “Auto‑forward” or “Mail Forwarding” in the admin console and point to the Zendesk address. |

> **Tip:** Add a **subject prefix** (e.g., `[Support]`) in the forwarding rule. This makes it easier to create triggers later that only fire on support‑related mail.

### 4. Test the Connection  

Send a test email from a personal address to the support address. Within a few seconds you should see a **new ticket** appear in Zendesk under **Tickets ▶ All**. Open the ticket and verify:

* **Subject** matches the email.
* **Requester** is the sender’s address.
* **Comments** contain the email body.

If the ticket does not appear, revisit the DNS and forwarding settings, then consult Zendesk’s **Help Center** for troubleshooting.

### 5. Keep Email Clean  

* **Spam filtering** – Enable Zendesk’s built‑in spam detection (Admin ▶ Channels ▶ Email ▶ Spam settings).  
* **Auto‑responses** – Create a **trigger** that sends a “We’ve received your email” reply, letting customers know you’re on it. (You already know how to build triggers from Chapter 5.)

---

## Enabling Zendesk Chat  

### 1. Activate the Chat Product  

1. From the **Admin** panel, select **Channels ▶ Chat**.  
2. Click **Start trial** (if you’re on a free trial) or **Buy now** to add the Chat add‑on to your subscription.  
3. Once activated, you’ll land on the **Chat dashboard**.

### 2. Create a Chat Widget  

A *widget* is the little chat button that appears on your website.  

1. Click **Settings ▶ Widget**.  
2. **Name** the widget (e.g., “Live Help”).  
3. Choose a **theme** (colors, logo) that matches your brand.  
4. Decide **placement** – the default is a floating button at the bottom‑right of the page.  

> **Tip:** Use the **Preview** pane to see how the widget looks before publishing.

### 3. Deploy the Widget Code  

1. In the widget screen, click **Copy code**.  
2. Paste the snippet just before the closing `</body>` tag on every page you want chat enabled.  
3. Save and publish the page.  

When you reload the page, the chat button should appear. Click it to start a test conversation; you’ll see the chat appear as a **new ticket** in Zendesk, labeled with the **Chat** channel.

### 4. Route Chats to the Right Agents  

1. Go to **Admin ▶ Channels ▶ Chat ▶ Routing**.  
2. **Add a queue** and assign it to a **Group** you created earlier (e.g., “Live‑Chat Support”).  
3. Enable **Skill‑based routing** if you have agents with specific expertise (e.g., “Billing”, “Technical”).  

Now incoming chats are automatically placed in the queue and shown to agents who belong to that group.

### 5. Configure Pre‑Chat and Offline Forms  

* **Pre‑chat form** – Ask for name, email, and order number before the chat starts. This information is stored in the ticket’s **custom fields** (you already know how to add custom fields from earlier chapters).  
* **Offline form** – When agents are unavailable, visitors can leave a message that becomes a **ticket** with a “Chat – Offline” status.

Both forms are edited under **Chat ▶ Settings ▶ Form**.

---

## Configuring Zendesk Talk (Phone)  

### 1. Activate Talk  

1. In **Admin**, select **Channels ▶ Talk**.  
2. Click **Start trial** or **Buy now** to add the Talk add‑on.  

### 2. Purchase or Port a Phone Number  

* **Buy a new number** – Choose a country, then click **Buy**.  
* **Port an existing number** – Follow Zendesk’s port‑in guide; you’ll need to provide a **Letter of Authorization** from your current carrier.  

The number appears under **Talk ▶ Numbers**.

### 3. Set Up Greetings and IVR  

**IVR (Interactive Voice Response)** lets callers navigate menus using their keypad.  

1. Click **IVR** in the Talk dashboard.  
2. **Add a greeting** (e.g., “Welcome to Acme Support. Press 1 for sales, 2 for technical help, 0 for an operator”).  
3. Record the greeting using the built‑in recorder or upload an MP3 file.  
4. Map each keypad option to a **queue** or **agent group**.  

### 4. Create Queues and Assign Agents  

1. Under **Talk ▶ Queues**, click **Add queue**.  
2. Name the queue (e.g., “Tech Support”).  
3. Assign a **Group** (the same group you used for chat if you want a unified voice‑and‑chat team).  

Agents added to the group will see incoming calls in the **Talk interface** and can answer them directly from the Zendesk UI.

### 5. Enable Call Recording and Voicemail  

* **Call recording** – Toggle **Enable recording** on the **Numbers** page. Recordings are attached to the ticket for later review.  
* **Voicemail** – Set up a **voicemail greeting** and define the **email address** where voicemails are sent (usually the same as your support email).  

### 6. Test the Phone Flow  

Dial the newly purchased number from a phone. Follow the IVR prompts and verify that:

* The call lands in the correct queue.  
* An agent can answer and see the **call details** (caller ID, IVR path).  
* After the call ends, a **ticket** is created with the **Talk** channel and includes the call recording (if enabled).  

If anything fails, double‑check the **routing rules** and ensure the agents are logged in to Talk.

---

## Integrating Social Media  

Zendesk can pull messages from **Facebook** and **Twitter** directly into tickets, letting agents reply without leaving the platform.

### 1. Connect a Facebook Page  

1. In **Admin**, go to **Channels ▶ Facebook**.  
2. Click **Connect Facebook Page**.  
3. A pop‑up will ask you to log into Facebook and **grant Zendesk permission** to manage your page’s messages.  
4. Choose the page you want to connect and confirm.  

> **Tip:** You need to be an **admin** of the Facebook Page to complete this step.

### 2. Connect a Twitter Account  

1. Still under **Channels**, select **Twitter**.  
2. Click **Connect Twitter** and log in with the account that has **Read & Write** access to the target handle.  
3. Authorize Zendesk to read direct messages, mentions, and send replies.  

### 3. Configure Social Settings  

* **Auto‑reply** – Create a **trigger** that sends a quick acknowledgment (“Thanks for reaching out! We’ll get back to you shortly”) the moment a social message becomes a ticket.  
* **Tagging** – Add a **tag** (e.g., `facebook`, `twitter`) via a trigger so you can filter social tickets in your views.  
* **Message routing** – Route social tickets to a specific **Group** (e.g., “Social Support”) using a trigger that checks the channel source.  

### 4. Replying to Customers  

Open any social ticket; you’ll see the original message and a **Reply** box. Type your response and click **Submit**. Zendesk will post the reply back to the original platform (Facebook or Twitter) and log it as a public comment in the ticket.

### 5. Handling Mentions vs. Direct Messages  

* **Mentions** – Appear as *public* tickets; you can choose to respond publicly or privately.  
* **Direct Messages** – Appear as *private* tickets; replies are sent as private messages on the platform.  

Use **triggers** to set the ticket **type** (`question`, `incident`, etc.) based on whether the message is public or private.

---

## Unified Ticket Management  

Now that all channels funnel into Zendesk, you can treat each interaction as a **ticket**—the same way you already manage email tickets.

### 1. Identify the Channel  

Every ticket automatically receives a **channel** attribute (`email`, `chat`, `talk`, `facebook`, `twitter`). You can surface this attribute in ticket **views**:

1. Go to **Admin ▶ Views**.  
2. Click **Add view** → **Conditions** → **Channel** = `chat`.  
3. Name the view “Live‑Chat Queue” and save.  

Repeat for each channel to create dedicated queues.

### 2. Use Triggers and Macros for Channel‑Specific Actions  

* **Trigger example** – When a ticket’s channel is `talk`, automatically set the **priority** to `high`.  
* **Macro example** – A “Quick Social Reply” macro that inserts a pre‑written thank‑you message and tags the ticket with `social`.  

Because you already know how to build triggers/macros (Chapter 5), simply add a **Condition** for **Channel**.

### 3. Assign Tickets to Groups  

When you created **Groups** earlier, you can now map each channel to a dedicated group:

| Channel | Recommended Group |
|---------|-------------------|
| Email   | Email Support |
| Chat    | Live‑Chat Support |
| Talk    | Phone Support |
| Facebook / Twitter | Social Support |

Use a **trigger** that sets the **Group** based on the channel, ensuring the right agents see the ticket in their **assigned view**.

### 4. Monitor Workload with Views  

Create a master view called “All Open Tickets” that shows every ticket regardless of channel. Then add **columns** for **Channel**, **Priority**, and **Group** so supervisors can quickly spot bottlenecks (e.g., a surge in phone calls).

---

## Best Practices for Multichannel Support  

| Practice | Why it matters | Quick implementation |
|----------|----------------|----------------------|
| **Consistent tone** | Customers expect the same brand voice across email, chat, phone, and social. | Draft a **brand style guide** and embed key phrases in macros. |
| **Channel‑specific SLAs** | Response expectations differ (e.g., chat should be answered within minutes, email within 24 h). | Use **triggers** to set **Due dates** based on channel. |
| **Avoid duplicate tickets** | A customer might email after a chat; you don’t want two separate tickets for the same issue. | Enable **ticket merging** (Admin ▶ Settings ▶ Tickets) and train agents to search by requester before creating a new ticket. |
| **Track channel performance** | Knowing which channel generates the most tickets helps allocate resources. | Later, Chapter 8 will show how to build reports; for now, regularly review the **Views** you created. |
| **Provide self‑service options** | Some customers prefer to find answers themselves, reducing ticket volume. | Link to your Help Center (Chapter 6) in chat pre‑chat forms and email signatures. |
| **Regularly update IVR and greetings** | Stale greetings can frustrate callers. | Schedule a quarterly review of Talk recordings and update scripts accordingly. |

---

## Key Takeaways  

* **All inbound communication**—email, live chat, phone calls, Facebook messages, and Twitter mentions—can be routed into **Zendesk tickets**, giving you a single place to manage support.  
* **Email**: Connect a custom address, set up DNS records, and forward mail; verify with a test ticket.  
* **Chat**: Activate the Chat product, design a widget, embed the code, and route chats to a dedicated group or skill queue.  
* **Talk (phone)**: Purchase/port a number, create IVR greetings, set up queues, and enable call recording for ticket attachment.  
* **Social**: Link your Facebook page and Twitter account, configure auto‑replies, tag tickets, and route them to a social‑support group.  
* Use **triggers**, **macros**, and **views** (already covered in earlier chapters) to automatically label, prioritize, and assign tickets based on their channel.  
* Apply **channel‑aware best practices**—consistent tone, SLA definitions, and regular content updates—to keep support efficient and customer‑friendly.  

By the end of this chapter, you should be able to **activate every major support channel**, **route each interaction to the right agents**, and **maintain a unified ticket workflow** that scales as your business grows.

modules.title: 8. Reporting and Analytics
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call  

Imagine your support manager, Maya, starts her day by opening her inbox. She sees a single email from the executive team: “Why did we miss the 24‑hour response SLA on 15 tickets yesterday? Explain.” Maya doesn’t have to dig through spreadsheets or ask the team for numbers—she can pull the exact data from Zendesk in seconds.  

This is the power of **Reporting and Analytics**: turning raw ticket activity into clear answers that keep your support operation running smoothly and your stakeholders confident.

In this chapter you’ll learn how to:

1. **Navigate the Reporting section** and make sense of the default dashboards Zendesk provides.  
2. **Create a custom ticket‑volume report** that you can filter by group or channel.  
3. **Set up SLA (Service Level Agreement) metrics** and keep an eye on compliance.  
4. **Schedule automated email reports** so the right people receive the right insights without manual effort.

All the steps assume you’ve already set up users, groups, and basic ticket fields (see Chapter 4) and have familiarized yourself with automations, triggers, and macros (Chapter 5).

---

## 1. Getting Started in the Reporting Section  

### 1.1 Where the Reporting hub lives  

1. From any Zendesk page, locate the **product tray** in the upper‑right corner (the grid of nine squares).  
2. Click the **“Reporting”** icon—its label reads *Reporting* and the icon resembles a bar chart.  
3. The **Reporting home** opens, showing three primary tabs: **Dashboards**, **Explore**, and **Insights** (the last two are available on higher‑tier plans; the default Dashboards tab works for all).

> **Tip:** If you do not see the Reporting icon, verify that your role includes the *Report Viewer* permission under **Admin → People → Roles** (refer back to Chapter 4).

### 1.2 Understanding the layout  

- **Navigation pane** (left): quick links to default dashboards, saved reports, and the *Create report* button.  
- **Main canvas** (center): visualizations—charts, tables, and key metrics.  
- **Filter bar** (top): global filters that affect every widget on the page (date range, organization, etc.).

The default view is a **“Support Overview”** dashboard that aggregates the most common performance indicators.

---

## 2. Exploring Default Dashboards  

Zendesk ships with several pre‑built dashboards designed for beginners. Below are the most useful for day‑to‑day support management.

| Dashboard | What it Shows | When to Use It |
|-----------|---------------|----------------|
| **Support Overview** | Ticket volume, first‑reply time, resolution time, CSAT (Customer Satisfaction) score. | Quick health check of the whole support line. |
| **Channel Breakdown** | Ticket counts split by **Email**, **Chat**, **Phone**, **Social**. | Identify which channel needs more staffing or training. |
| **Group Performance** | Tickets assigned, solved, and pending per **Group**. | Compare productivity across teams (e.g., *Technical Support* vs *Billing*). |
| **SLA Compliance** | Percentage of tickets meeting each SLA target (e.g., *First Reply* ≤ 4 h). | Spot SLA breaches before they affect customers. |

### 2.1 Interacting with a dashboard  

1. **Hover** over any chart to see exact numbers.  
2. Click the **filter icon** (funnel) on a widget to drill down—e.g., view only “Open” tickets in the *Channel Breakdown*.  
3. Use the **date picker** in the top‑right to switch from “Last 7 days” to “Last month” or a custom range.

These interactions are **instantaneous**; Zendesk recalculates the data on the fly, giving you a live view of your support operation.

---

## 3. Building a Custom Ticket‑Volume Report  

Default dashboards give you a high‑level picture, but often you need a report that answers a specific question—like “How many tickets did the *Luna Loom* support group receive via chat last week?”

### 3.1 Starting a new report  

1. In the Reporting home, click **“Create report”** (top‑right).  
2. Choose **“Ticket volume”** as the report type. This template automatically includes a **count of tickets** and a **date histogram** (tickets per day).  

### 3.2 Adding filters  

Zendesk lets you slice the data with **filters**—think of them as “questions you ask the data.”  

- **Group filter** – selects tickets owned by a particular group.  
- **Channel filter** – selects tickets created through a specific channel (Email, Chat, etc.).  

To add a filter:

1. Click **“Add filter”** in the filter bar.  
2. From the dropdown, select **“Group”**, then type the group name (e.g., *Luna Loom*).  
3. Click **“Add another filter”**, choose **“Channel”**, and pick *Chat*.  

You’ll now see a chart that only counts tickets meeting both criteria.

### 3.3 Choosing a visualization  

- **Bar chart** – good for comparing daily totals.  
- **Line chart** – shows trends over time.  
- **Table** – lists raw numbers for export.  

Select the chart icon that matches the story you want to tell. For a weekly snapshot, a **bar chart** works well.

### 3.4 Saving the report  

1. Click **“Save”** at the top of the canvas.  
2. Give it a clear name, e.g., *“Chat tickets – Luna Loom – Weekly”*.  
3. Choose a folder (e.g., *Team Reports*) so teammates can locate it later.  

Now the report appears under **“Saved reports”** and can be accessed anytime without rebuilding it.

---

## 4. Filtering by Group or Channel – A Step‑by‑Step Walkthrough  

Let’s walk through a concrete scenario: **You need to prove that the *Technical Support* group handled more than 200 email tickets last month.**

1. **Open** the Reporting home and click **Create report → Ticket volume**.  
2. **Set the date range** to *Last month* using the date picker.  
3. **Add a Group filter**:  
   - Click **Add filter → Group**.  
   - Type *Technical Support* and select it.  
4. **Add a Channel filter**:  
   - Click **Add filter → Channel**.  
   - Choose *Email*.  
5. **Choose a Table visualization** (so you can see the exact count).  
6. **Run** the report (the canvas updates automatically).  
7. The table now shows a single row with the total ticket count—let’s say **215**.  

You can **export** the table to CSV by clicking the **download icon** next to the table, then attach the file to Maya’s email reply.

> **Note:** Filters are *cumulative*—each new filter narrows the data set further. Removing a filter widens the view again.

---

## 5. Understanding SLA Metrics  

### 5.1 What is an SLA?  

**SLA (Service Level Agreement)** is a contract‑like promise that defines how quickly your support team must respond to or resolve a ticket. Common SLA targets include:

- **First Reply** – Time from ticket creation to the first public reply.  
- **Resolution** – Time from creation to ticket status “Solved”.  
- **Urgent Ticket** – Faster response for high‑priority tickets.

Zendesk stores SLA definitions under **Admin → Business Rules → SLAs**.

### 5.2 Where SLA data lives in reports  

When you add an **“SLA compliance”** widget to a dashboard, Zendesk automatically calculates:

- **% of tickets meeting the SLA** (e.g., 92% of first‑reply SLA met).  
- **Average breach time** (how long after the deadline tickets remained open).  

These metrics appear as **kpi cards** (large numbers) and as **trend graphs** over selected periods.

---

## 6. Setting Up SLA Goals  

### 6.1 Defining an SLA rule  

1. Navigate to **Admin → Business Rules → SLAs**.  
2. Click **“Add SLA”**.  
3. Fill in the fields:  

| Field | Example Value |
|-------|---------------|
| **Name** | *Standard First Reply* |
| **Target** | *First reply ≤ 4 hours* |
| **Applies to** | *All tickets* (or limit by **Group**, **Priority**, **Channel**) |
| **Conditions** | *Ticket status = New* |
| **Business hours** | *Mon‑Fri, 9 am‑5 pm* (optional) |

4. Click **Save**.  

Now every ticket that meets the conditions will be evaluated against this SLA.

### 6.2 Linking SLA to reporting  

Zendesk automatically adds the new SLA to the **SLA Compliance** dashboard. If you want a dedicated view:

1. In Reporting, click **Create report → SLA compliance**.  
2. Add a filter for the SLA you just created (e.g., *Standard First Reply*).  
3. Save the report as *“First Reply SLA – Monthly”*.

---

## 7. Monitoring SLA Compliance  

### 7.1 Real‑time alerts vs. periodic reports  

- **Real‑time alerts** (set up via **Triggers**) can email you instantly when a ticket breaches an SLA. This is useful for urgent escalations.  
- **Periodic reports** give a broader picture—how many tickets breached the SLA over the past week, which groups are most affected, etc.

### 7.2 Using the SLA dashboard  

Open the **SLA Compliance** dashboard and look for:

- **KPI cards** showing the overall compliance percentage (e.g., 94%).  
- **Breaches by group** chart—spot groups that repeatedly miss targets.  
- **Trend line** for each SLA metric—detect seasonal slumps (e.g., higher breach rates on weekends).

If a KPI falls below your internal threshold (say 90%), you can drill down:

1. Click the **breach chart**.  
2. Add a **Group filter** to see which team is responsible.  
3. Export the filtered list for a follow‑up meeting.

---

## 8. Automating Report Delivery  

Manual export and email is error‑prone. Zendzend’s **Scheduled Reports** feature lets you send a report on a recurring basis.

### 8.1 Creating a scheduled email  

1. Open the saved report you want to automate (e.g., *“Chat tickets – Luna Loom – Weekly”*).  
2. Click **“Schedule”** (clock icon near the report name).  
3. Fill out the schedule form:

| Setting | Example |
|--------|---------|
| **Frequency** | *Weekly* |
| **Day** | *Monday* |
| **Time** | *08:00 AM* (your local time zone) |
| **Recipients** | *maya@company.com, team‑lead@company.com* |
| **Format** | *PDF* (or CSV/Excel) |
| **Subject line** | *Weekly Chat Ticket Summary – Luna Loom* |
| **Message** | *Hi team, please find attached the latest chat ticket volume…* |

4. Click **Save**.  

Zendesk will now generate the report at the specified time and email it automatically.

### 8.2 Managing scheduled reports  

- **View all schedules** under **Reporting → Scheduled reports**.  
- **Edit** a schedule by clicking the pencil icon.  
- **Disable** a schedule temporarily (useful during holidays).  

> **Tip:** Keep the recipient list short and relevant. Too many inboxes dilute the impact of the data.

---

## 9. Practical Tips & Common Pitfalls  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | How to Avoid |
|---------|----------------|--------------|
| **Using “All tickets” when you only need “Solved”** | Default reports include every ticket status, inflating volume numbers. | Add a **Status filter** (e.g., *Solved* or *Closed*) before saving the report. |
| **Over‑filtering** | Adding too many filters can result in empty charts, making the report look broken. | Start with one filter, preview the data, then add another only if needed. |
| **Ignoring time zones** | SLA calculations use the business‑hour time zone you set; mismatched zones cause unexpected breaches. | Verify the **Business Hours** time zone matches your support team’s location. |
| **Scheduling reports at peak hours** | Recipients may miss the email if it lands during busy periods. | Choose early‑morning or late‑afternoon slots when inbox traffic is lower. |
| **Not naming reports clearly** | Team members can’t find the right report in the saved list. | Adopt a naming convention: *[Metric] – [Group] – [Period]* (e.g., *First Reply SLA – Support – Monthly*). |

---

## 10. Bringing It All Together – A Mini‑Project  

**Goal:** Provide the executive team with a weekly snapshot that includes:**

- Total tickets per channel.  
- Ticket volume for the *Luna Loom* group (filtered by channel).  
- First‑reply SLA compliance percentage.  

**Steps:**

1. **Create three separate reports** using the processes above:  
   - *Channel Breakdown – Weekly* (default dashboard).  
   - *Luna Loom Ticket Volume – Weekly* (custom ticket‑volume report).  
   - *First Reply SLA – Weekly* (SLA compliance report).  
2. **Add each report to a new dashboard**:  
   - In Reporting, click **“Create dashboard”**, name it *Executive Weekly Summary*.  
   - Drag the three saved reports onto the canvas, arranging them for easy scanning.  
3. **Schedule the dashboard**:  
   - Click **“Schedule”** on the dashboard view.  
   - Set frequency to **Weekly**, day **Monday**, time **07:30 AM**, recipients **exec‑team@company.com**.  
   - Choose **PDF** format and write a brief note: “Weekly support performance – see attached.”  
4. **Test** the schedule by clicking **“Send now”** to verify the email lands correctly.  

Now, every Monday morning Maya’s executives receive a concise, visual summary that answers their “why did we miss the SLA?” question before anyone even asks.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **Reporting** hub is accessed via the product tray and houses default dashboards, custom reports, and scheduled email options.  
- **Default dashboards** (Support Overview, Channel Breakdown, Group Performance, SLA Compliance) give instant insight into overall support health.  
- To answer specific questions, **create a custom ticket‑volume report** and filter it by **Group** and **Channel**.  
- **SLAs** are defined under Admin → Business Rules → SLAs; once created they automatically appear in the SLA Compliance dashboard.  
- **Monitoring SLA compliance** involves both real‑time alerts (triggers) and periodic reports to spot trends and breaches.  
- **Scheduled reports** automate distribution of PDFs/CSVs to stakeholders, ensuring data arrives on time without manual effort.  
- Use clear naming, avoid over‑filtering, and align time zones to keep reports accurate and useful.  

With these tools, you can turn raw ticket data into actionable intelligence, keep your SLAs on track, and keep every stakeholder informed—just like Maya did.

modules.title: 9. Ongoing Optimization and Best Practices
modules.content:
Improving your support isn’t a one-time setup—it’s an ongoing process. The tools you’ve learned so far—ticket workflows, automations, knowledge base, and reports—aren’t meant to sit unchanged. Just like a garden, a Zendesk setup needs regular care to stay efficient and effective.

Imagine Luna Loom, a small online retailer, has been using Zendesk for months. Their ticket volume has grown, but so has their backlog. Agents are spending more time manually reassigning tickets and searching for answers. Customers are waiting longer, and satisfaction scores are slipping. What should they do?

This chapter shows how to keep Zendesk performing at its best with continuous review and small, smart improvements. You’ll learn how to find bottlenecks, use feedback to make changes, keep your help center fresh, and review your automations regularly. These practices ensure your support stays fast, accurate, and scalable—without needing a full rebuild every few months.

By the end, you’ll have a clear routine for maintaining a high-performing Zendesk, even as your business grows.

---

## Start with a Ticket Audit: Find the Hidden Slowdowns

A ticket audit is a review of recent tickets to spot patterns, delays, or inefficiencies in your workflow. Think of it as a health check for your support process.

### How to Run a Basic Ticket Audit

1. **Pick a time range** – Start with the last 7–30 days. Too short, and you won’t see patterns. Too long, and the data may not reflect current processes.
2. **Filter tickets by status** – Focus on **open**, **pending**, and **solved** tickets. These reveal where work is piling up.
3. **Look for these red flags:**
   - **Tickets stuck in one status too long** – e.g., “pending” for more than 24 hours.
   - **Frequent reassignments** – a ticket moved between groups or agents multiple times.
   - **Long resolution times** – compare average time to industry benchmarks if you have them.
4. **Group by agent or channel** – Is one agent consistently slower? Are chat tickets resolved faster than email?

> **Tip:** Use Zendesk’s built-in filters and views to create a custom “Audit View.” Save it so you can reuse it each month.

For example, Luna Loom might find that **30% of tickets** are being reassigned because the wrong group was assigned initially. That points to a training or routing issue—not a people problem.

---

## Build Feedback Loops: Use Surveys to Guide Improvements

Customer feedback is your compass. Zendesk’s **satisfaction surveys** (CSAT) give direct input from users on every ticket. But it’s not enough to collect the data—you need to act on it.

### How to Set Up and Use CSAT Surveys

1. **Enable CSAT in Admin Settings** → **Customer Satisfaction** → Turn on “Allow customers to rate this ticket.”
2. **Choose when to send the survey** – After the ticket is solved, or after every reply.
3. **Review results regularly** – Check the **CSAT report** in Zendesk Analytics (from Chapter 8).
4. **Look for patterns:**
   - Low scores on specific ticket types (e.g., refunds, cancellations).
   - Repeated negative comments about a particular agent.
   - High scores on certain knowledge base articles.

> **Tip:** Add a custom survey question: “What could we have done better?” This gives qualitative insight.

Luna Loom noticed that **42% of low CSAT scores** were linked to slow responses on weekend tickets. They realized their weekend coverage was inconsistent. By adjusting agent schedules and setting weekend SLAs, they improved satisfaction by 22% in one month.

---

## Keep Your Knowledge Base Clean: A Living Resource

A stale knowledge base is worse than no knowledge base. Articles that are outdated, hard to find, or incorrect erode trust and increase ticket volume.

### How to Maintain Knowledge Base Hygiene

1. **Assign ownership** – One person (or team) should be responsible for reviewing articles each quarter.
2. **Create a review checklist:**
   - Is the information still accurate?
   - Are links working?
   - Does the article match current product or policy changes?
   - Is it easy to understand for beginners?
3. **Use article labels and categories** – Helps agents and customers find relevant info faster.
4. **Retire old articles** – Don’t just delete—redirect users to updated versions when possible.
5. **Track usage data** – Check which articles are viewed most (and least). High views but low resolution? That article might need improvement.

> **Tip:** Schedule a “knowledge base cleanup day” every quarter. Block 2–4 hours to review and update.

Luna Loom found an article on “How to return a product” that still referenced their old return address. After updating it, ticket volume on returns dropped by 15%.

---

## Review Automations, Triggers, and Macros Quarterly

Automations, triggers, and macros are powerful—but they can become outdated or redundant over time. A monthly coupon code trigger from a past promotion might still be firing, clogging your system with irrelevant tickets.

### How to Audit Your Automation Stack

1. **List all active automations, triggers, and macros.**
   - In Admin → **Objects and rules** → Automations, Triggers, Macros.
2. **Check for these issues:**
   - **Orphaned rules** – Rules that no longer apply (e.g., expired promotions).
   - **Overlapping rules** – Two triggers doing the same thing, causing confusion.
   - **Unused macros** – Macros created but never applied.
3. **Test each rule** – Change one variable in a test ticket to confirm it triggers as expected.
4. **Document changes** – Keep a simple log of what you change and why.

> **Tip:** Use meaningful names for rules—e.g., “Auto-assign Tier 2: Billing Issues” instead of “Trigger 7.”

Luna Loom discovered a “Happy Birthday” trigger that was still sending discount codes to customers who hadn’t made a purchase in over a year. Removing it reduced irrelevant notifications by 90%.

---

## Use Reports to Spot Trends and Justify Changes

You already know how to pull reports (from Chapter 8). Now, use them to guide your optimization.

### Key Reports for Ongoing Improvement

| Report | Why It Matters | How to Act |
|-------|----------------|-----------|
| **Ticket Volume by Channel** | Shows where support is growing | Adjust staffing or automate responses in high-volume channels |
| **First Reply Time** | Measures responsiveness | Identify agents below target; offer training or adjust workload |
| **Resolution Time** | Tracks efficiency | Look for tickets taking too long—are they complex, or is something blocking progress? |
| **CSAT by Agent** | Highlights performance gaps | Provide coaching to low-scoring agents or reassign tickets they struggle with |
| **Knowledge Base Views** | Reveals gaps in self-service | Improve or create articles where users are stuck |

> **Tip:** Set up **scheduled reports** to email you weekly or monthly. You’ll catch issues faster.

---

## Build a Routine: Make Optimization a Habit

Optimization isn’t a one-time task. It’s a rhythm. Here’s a simple monthly routine to keep your Zendesk running smoothly:

### Monthly Optimization Checklist

- [ ] Run a **ticket audit** – Review 20–30 solved tickets for patterns.
- [ ] Check **CSAT scores** – Look for sudden drops or trends.
- [ ] Update **knowledge base articles** – Review top-viewed and lowest-rated articles.
- [ ] Audit **automations and macros** – Remove or fix outdated rules.
- [ ] Review **agent performance** – Compare key metrics against goals.
- [ ] Update **views and SLAs** – Adjust if response times are slipping.

Set a recurring calendar invite. Even 30 minutes a month can prevent bigger issues down the road.

---

## Real-World Scenario: From Reactive to Proactive at Luna Loom

Luna Loom started with a reactive approach: they fixed issues as they came up. After six months, they realized they were always playing catch-up.

They began with a ticket audit. They found that **25% of tickets** were about the same issue: “How do I track my order?” Their knowledge base had an outdated article.

They:
- Updated the article with accurate steps and screenshots.
- Added a **macro** for agents to quickly paste the link.
- Set up an **automation** to suggest the article in the first reply when the word “track” appeared.

Within two weeks, tickets about order tracking dropped by 40%. Customer satisfaction on those tickets rose from 65% to 89%.

They made this a habit. Now, every month, they review their top 5 ticket types and ask: *Can we reduce these with better self-service or automation?*

---

## ## Key Takeaways

- **Use CSAT surveys** to gather direct feedback and guide improvements.
- **Clean and update your knowledge base** quarterly to maintain accuracy and usefulness.
- **Audit automations, triggers, and macros** every quarter to remove outdated or redundant rules.

# Chapter 1: 1. Account Setup and Initial Configuration

## Getting Started: Why the First Ticket Matters  

Imagine you’ve just launched your online boutique, **Luna Loom**, and the first customer writes:

That email is the moment you’ll know whether your support process is ready for real‑world demand. Setting up a **Zendesk** account correctly from day one turns that single email into a tracked, visible **ticket**—the foundation of every organized support interaction.

This chapter walks you through every step needed to get that first ticket into Zendesk, from signing up for a trial or paid account to configuring your company’s profile, branding, timezone, and default support email address. By the end, you’ll have a live Zendesk instance that can receive, display, and respond to customer inquiries, ready for the next steps in the learning path.

---

## 1. Creating Your Zendesk Account  

### 1.1 Choose Between a Trial and a Paid Subscription  

| Option | What You Get | When It’s Best For |
|--------|--------------|--------------------|
| **Free Trial (30 days)** | Full access to the selected plan’s features, no credit‑card required | Exploring the platform, short‑term projects, or proof‑of‑concept |
| **Paid Subscription** | Ongoing access, billing on a monthly or annual basis | Established businesses, long‑term support, or when you need guaranteed uptime |

> **Tip:** Even if you intend to pay later, start with the free trial. You can upgrade to a paid plan at any time without losing data.

### 1.2 Step‑by‑Step Account Creation  

1. **Visit the Zendesk Sign‑up Page**  
   - URL: `https://www.zendesk.com/register/`  
   - Select **“Start free trial”** or **“Buy now”** depending on your choice.

2. **Enter Basic Information**  
   - **Name** – Your personal or company contact name.  
   - **Work email** – Must be a valid address you can access (used for verification).  
   - **Phone number** – Optional, but useful for account recovery.

3. **Pick a Subdomain**  
   - Zendesk creates a unique subdomain in the form `yourcompany.zendesk.com`.  
   - Choose something short, memorable, and aligned with your brand (e.g., `lunaloomboutique.zendesk.com`).

4. **Select a Support Plan**  
   - You’ll see the plan options (see Section 2). Choose one now or skip and decide later; you can always change it from the **Admin** console.

5. **Agree to Terms & Submit**  
   - Review the **Terms of Service** and **Privacy Policy**. Tick the box and click **“Create account.”**

6. **Email Verification**  
   - Zendesk sends a verification link to the email you entered.  
   - Open the email, click **“Verify my email”**, and you’ll be redirected to the Zendesk dashboard.

> **What If the Email Doesn’t Arrive?**  
> - Check your spam/junk folder.  
> - Ensure you typed the address correctly.  
> - If still missing, use the **“Resend verification”** link on the login page.

---

## 2. Selecting the Right Support Plan  

Zendesk offers several plans, each adding layers of functionality. Below is a simplified overview (prices are illustrative; check Zendesk’s website for current rates).

| Plan | Core Features | Typical Use‑Case |
|------|---------------|------------------|
| **Essential** | Ticketing, email channel, basic reporting | Small teams (1‑5 agents) handling low volume |
| **Team** | All Essential features + collaboration tools, SLA (Service Level Agreement) management | Growing teams (5‑15 agents) needing response‑time guarantees |
| **Professional** | Adds custom ticket fields, advanced automations, multi‑channel (chat, social) | Mid‑size businesses (15‑50 agents) with diverse support channels |
| **Enterprise** | Full suite – AI‑powered bots, advanced analytics, custom roles | Large organizations (>50 agents) with complex workflows |

### 2.1 Matching Plan Features to Business Needs  

1. **Ticket Volume** – Estimate how many tickets you expect per month.  
   - < 500 tickets → Essential or Team.  
   - 500‑5,000 tickets → Professional.  
   - > 5,000 tickets → Enterprise.

2. **Channel Mix** – If you plan to support **chat, phone, or social media** soon, choose a plan that already includes those channels (Professional or Enterprise). You can add channels later, but starting with the right plan saves migration effort.

3. **SLA Requirements** – Do you need to promise a **“first response within 2 hours”**? SLA management is only available from the **Team** plan upward.

4. **Customization** – Custom ticket fields, branding, and role‑based permissions become essential as your support operation scales. These are part of Professional and Enterprise.

5. **Budget Constraints** – If you’re a startup with tight cash flow, start with **Essential** and upgrade as revenue grows.

### 2.2 Changing Plans Later  

- **Upgrade** – From the **Admin > Subscription** page, click **“Change plan.”** Follow the prompts; the change is effective immediately.  
- **Downgrade** – Allowed only after the current billing cycle ends. Zendesk will retain your data, but features not supported by the lower plan become inactive.

> **Pro Tip:** Keep a spreadsheet of your projected ticket volume and support channel usage for the next 12 months. Review it quarterly and adjust your plan before the next billing cycle.

---

## 3. Configuring Your Company Profile  

A well‑filled company profile makes your Zendesk instance feel like an extension of your brand.

### 3.1 Accessing the Profile Settings  

1. Click the **gear icon** (Admin) in the left sidebar.  
2. Under **“Account”**, select **“Account Settings.”**  
3. You’ll see tabs for **General**, **Branding**, **Localization**, and **Security**.

### 3.2 General Information  

| Field | What to Enter | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Company name** | Full legal name (e.g., *Luna Loom Boutique LLC*) | Appears in ticket notifications and Help Center. |
| **Domain** | Your public website domain (e.g., `lunaloomboutique.com`) | Used for email routing and branding. |
| **Support email** | Default address (e.g., `support@lunaloomboutique.com`) – set up later in Section 4. | Central point of contact for customers. |
| **Phone number** | Optional, for admin alerts. | Helps with account recovery or two‑factor authentication. |

### 3.3 Branding  

1. **Logo** – Upload a PNG or SVG (max 300 KB). This appears in the header of the Help Center and in email footers.  
2. **Primary color** – Choose a hex code that matches your brand (e.g., `#4A90E2`). Zendesk uses this color for button accents and ticket status tags.  
3. **Favicon** – Small icon displayed in browser tabs. Upload a 16 × 16 px image.

> **Best Practice:** Use the same logo and color scheme you use on your website. Consistency reinforces brand trust.

### 3.4 Localization (Timezone & Language)  

1. **Timezone** – Select the region where your support team operates (e.g., **“America/New_York – Eastern Time (US & Canada)”**). All timestamps on tickets and reports will use this timezone.  
2. **Default language** – Choose the language for Zendesk’s UI and system notifications (e.g., **English (US)**). You can enable additional languages later for multilingual support.

> **Note:** Changing the timezone after tickets have been created does **not** alter the original timestamps; it only affects how new timestamps are displayed.

---

## 4. Setting Up the Default Support Email Address  

The email address you give customers (e.g., `support@lunaloomboutique.com`) is the gateway for tickets to enter Zendesk.

### 4.1 Create the Email Alias  

1. **Log in to your domain’s email provider** (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, etc.).  
2. **Create a new mailbox or alias** named **support**.  
   - If you use an alias, forward all incoming mail to a real mailbox that you control.  
   - Ensure the mailbox can receive **HTML** messages (most modern providers do).

### 4.2 Configure DNS Records (Optional but Recommended)  

To improve deliverability and prevent tickets from being marked as spam, add the following DNS records for your domain:

| Record Type | Name | Value | Purpose |
|-------------|------|-------|---------|
| **SPF** | `@` (or your domain) | `v=spf1 include:mail.zendesk.com ~all` | Authorizes Zendesk to send email on your behalf. |
| **DKIM** | `zendesk._domainkey` | Provided by Zendesk (a long string) | Cryptographically signs outgoing mail, proving it’s authentic. |
| **DMARC** | `_dmarc` | `v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:postmaster@yourdomain.com` | Gives you visibility into spoofing attempts. |

> **How to Add Records:**  
> - In your domain registrar’s DNS management console, click **“Add Record.”**  
> - Choose the correct type (TXT for SPF & DMARC, CNAME for DKIM).  
> - Paste the values exactly as shown. Propagation can take up to 48 hours, but most changes appear within a few minutes.

### 4.3 Connect the Email to Zendesk  

1. In Zendesk, go to **Admin > Channels > Email**.  
2. Click **“Add address”** and type **support@lunaloomboutique.com**.  
3. Choose **“Forwarding”** (recommended) or **“Direct”**:
   - **Forwarding** – You forward incoming mail from your provider to a unique Zendesk address (e.g., `support@lunaloomboutique.zendesk.com`). This method keeps the original mailbox active for internal use.  
   - **Direct** – Zendesk fetches mail via POP/IMAP; more complex and usually unnecessary for beginners.

4. **Verify Ownership** – Zendesk sends a verification email to the address you entered. Open the email (from `support@lunaloomboutique.com`) and click the verification link.

5. **Set as Default** – In the same **Email** settings page, click the three‑dot menu next to the address and select **“Set as default support address.”** This makes the address the primary source for all new tickets.

### 4.4 Test the Email Integration  

1. From a personal email account, send a message to `support@lunaloomboutique.com` with the subject **“Test ticket – please ignore.”**  
2. Log in to Zendesk, navigate to the **Views** section, and look for the **“Unassigned”** or **“All Unsolved Tickets”** view.  
3. The email you just sent should appear as a new ticket, with the subject line and body intact.

> **If the ticket doesn’t appear:**  
> - Confirm the forwarding rule is active and points to the correct Zendesk address.  
> - Check the **Email Logs** in Zendesk (Admin > Channels > Email > Logs) for any error messages.  
> - Verify DNS records if you receive a bounce or spam notice.

---

## 5. Creating and Managing Your First Ticket  

Now that the support email is live, let’s walk through the full ticket lifecycle—from arrival to resolution.

### 5.1 Ticket Creation Flow  

1. **Customer sends email** → Zendesk receives it via the configured address.  
2. **Zendesk parses the email** → Generates a ticket with:
   - **Subject** (email subject line)  
   - **Description** (email body)  
   - **Requester** (customer’s email address)  
   - **Status** set to **“New.”**  

3. **Ticket appears in the “Unassigned” view** (or any view you configure later).  

### 5.2 Responding to the Ticket  

1. Click the ticket to open the **Ticket Viewer**.  
2. In the **Comment** field, type your reply (e.g., “Hi Emily, thanks for reaching out! We can exchange the dress for a size M at no extra charge. Please let us know your preferred address.”).  
3. **Choose “Public”** to send the response to the customer, or “Private” for internal notes.  
4. Click **“Submit”**. Zendesk automatically sends the reply to the customer’s email address, preserving the ticket thread.

### 5.3 Updating Ticket Status  

- **New → Open** – Happens automatically when an agent (you) first responds.  
- **Open → Pending** – Use when you’ve asked the customer for more information.  
- **Pending → Solved** – Mark as solved once the issue is resolved.  
- **Solved → Closed** – After a configurable period (default 30 days), tickets auto‑close; you can also close manually.

> **Best Practice:** Keep the status accurate. It drives reporting, SLA calculations, and workload visibility for the whole team.

### 5.4 Adding Internal Notes  

Sometimes you need to share information with teammates without notifying the customer (e.g., “Check inventory for size M”). Use the **“Private”** comment type, which appears only in the ticket’s internal history.

### 5.5 Assigning the Ticket  

If you have multiple agents or groups (covered later), you can assign the ticket to a specific **agent** or **group**:

1. Click the **Assignee** dropdown in the ticket header.  
2. Select the appropriate name.  
3. The ticket moves to the assignee’s **“My Open Tickets”** view.

For now, with a single‑agent setup, you’ll simply keep the ticket **unassigned** or assign it to yourself.

### 5.6 Closing the Loop  

After you set the ticket to **Solved**, you’ll receive a **“Ticket solved”** email notification (if you have email notifications enabled). The customer will also get a copy of the final conversation, confirming that the issue is resolved.

---  

## 6. Quick‑Start Checklist  

| ✅ | Task | How to Verify |

| 1 | Create Zendesk account (trial or paid) | Logged‑in dashboard appears |
| 2 | Verify email address | Clicked verification link in inbox |

---

## 7. Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Problem | Why It Happens | Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----|
| **Email not converting to tickets** | Forwarding rule points to the wrong Zendesk address or verification not completed. | Re‑check the forwarding address and click the verification link again. |
| **Tickets show up with the wrong timezone** | Timezone set to UTC or a different region in **Account Settings**. | Update the timezone to your local business zone (Admin > Account Settings > Localization). |

| **Unable to change plan later** | Attempting to downgrade before the billing cycle ends. | Wait until the current cycle completes, then downgrade via **Admin > Subscription**. |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Start with a live Zendesk account**—whether a free trial or paid subscription—by creating a subdomain and verifying your email.  
- **Select a plan** that aligns with expected ticket volume, channel mix, SLA needs, and budget; you can upgrade later.  
- **Fill out the company profile**: name, logo, brand colors, and timezone. Consistent branding makes the support experience feel seamless.  
- **Configure a default support email address** (e.g., `support@yourdomain.com`) and, if possible, set up SPF/DKIM/DKIM DNS records to keep messages out of spam folders.

With these foundational steps completed, your Zendesk instance is ready to handle real customer inquiries, and you’re prepared to dive deeper into ticket management, automation, and multichannel support in the upcoming chapters.

# Chapter 2: 2. Navigating the Zendesk Interface

## A New Agent’s First Login

Maya just finished her onboarding session. She’s been given a **Free Trial** of Zendesk, her manager has set her up with an **Agent** role, and she’s ready to start helping customers. When she clicks the link in her welcome email and enters her credentials, a clean screen greets her. The question she asks herself is simple: *“Where do I go to see the tickets that need my attention?”*  

The answer lies in the layout of the Zendesk interface. Understanding the placement of the **Dashboard**, **Tickets**, **Views**, and **Reporting** areas—and how to move among them—will turn Maya’s first nervous clicks into confident navigation.

---

## 1. The Zendesk Interface at a Glance  

Zendesk’s web UI is built around two primary navigation components:

| Component | What It Looks Like | Primary Purpose |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|
| **Top navigation bar** | Horizontal strip across the top of the screen, usually dark‑blue or gray. | Global actions (search, notifications, profile, help, and switching between major sections). |
| **Left sidebar** | Vertical column on the left, collapsible in many plans. | Quick access to core objects (Dashboard, Tickets, Views, Reporting, Apps). |

Below the sidebar sits the **main workspace**, where the content of the selected section appears. A thin footer may contain legal links or a “Powered by Zendesk” badge, but it does not affect navigation.

### 1.1. Top Navigation Bar Details  

1. **Search bar** – Type keywords, ticket IDs, or user names to locate items instantly.  
2. **Global notifications** – Bell icon shows recent system alerts (e.g., new tickets, SLA breaches).  
3. **Profile menu** – Click your avatar to reach **My Settings**, **Switch account**, **Log out**, and **Help Center**.  
4. **Product switcher** – In larger organizations, a dropdown lets you jump between Zendesk **Support**, **Chat**, **Talk**, or **Guide** products.

### 1.2. Left Sidebar Sections  

| Icon | Label | Typical Content |
|------|-------|-----------------|
| 🏠 | **Dashboard** | High‑level metrics, recent activity, and customizable widgets. |
| 🎟️ | **Tickets** | List of all tickets, filter bar, bulk actions. |
| 👀 | **Views** | Saved filters (e.g., “Open – High Priority”) that act as personal worklists. |
| 📊 | **Reporting** | Pre‑built and custom reports, analytics charts, export options. |
| ⚙️ | **Admin** (visible only to admins) | Settings for users, groups, channels, automations, etc. |

When Maya clicks **Tickets**, the main workspace loads a table of all tickets she can see, based on her permissions. If she later clicks **Views**, the same workspace swaps to show the list of her saved worklists.

---

## 2. Identifying the Core Areas  

### 2.1. Dashboard – Your “Control Center”  

The **Dashboard** is the first page most users land on after logging in. It provides a snapshot of:

- **Ticket volume** (today, this week, this month)  
- **SLA compliance** (percentage of tickets answered within the promised time)  
- **Agent activity** (how many tickets each agent has closed)  

All widgets are **drag‑and‑drop**, so you can rearrange them to match your daily priorities. For a new agent, the default dashboard often includes:

- **Open tickets** count  
- **Pending tickets** count  
- **Recent satisfaction scores**  

Maya can add a widget for “My tickets awaiting response” to keep her focus narrow.

### 2.2. Tickets – The Heart of Support  

The **Tickets** section is a searchable table that lists every ticket in the system (subject to your role’s permissions). Columns typically include:

- **Ticket ID** – Unique number used in URLs and communications.  
- **Requester** – The end‑user who opened the ticket.  
- **Subject** – Brief description of the issue.  
- **Status** – Open, Pending, Solved, Closed.  
- **Priority** – Low, Normal, High, Urgent.  

You can customize which columns appear via the **Display settings** (gear icon) at the top of the table.

### 2.3. Views – Your Personal Worklists  

**Views** are saved filters that present tickets meeting specific criteria. Think of them as “smart folders.” A typical agent might have:

- **My Open Tickets** – Tickets assigned to the agent that are still open.  
- **High‑Priority Unassigned** – Urgent tickets that no one has claimed yet.  
- **Tickets Awaiting Customer** – Tickets where the last public comment came from the agent, and the status is **Pending**.  

Creating a view involves defining:

1. **Conditions** (e.g., Status = Open, Priority = High)  
2. **Columns** to display (Ticket ID, Subject, Group, etc.)  
3. **Sorting** order (most recent first, highest priority first, etc.)  

Admins can share views with entire groups; agents can create personal views for themselves.

### 2.4. Reporting – Turning Data into Insight  

The **Reporting** area houses both **pre‑built reports** (e.g., “Ticket Solved Times”) and **custom reports** you can build with the **Explore** tool. While agents usually view reports in read‑only mode, admins can design dashboards that surface key performance indicators (KPIs) for the whole support team.

Key report types include:

- **Ticket volume trends** (by channel, by day)  
- **First‑reply time** (how quickly agents answer)  
- **Customer satisfaction (CSAT)** scores  

Reports can be exported as CSV files for deeper analysis or scheduled to be emailed to stakeholders.

---

## 3. Moving Between Sections – The Navigation Workflow  

### 3.1. Using the Sidebar  

1. **Locate the icon** you need (e.g., 🎟️ for Tickets).  
2. **Click** once – the main workspace updates instantly.  
3. **Hover** over an icon to see a tooltip if you’re unsure of its meaning.  

The sidebar can be **collapsed** (arrow at the top) to free screen real estate. Collapsing does not hide the icons; it merely shrinks the labels. Maya can toggle this as she works on a wide monitor.

### 3.2. Switching via the Top Bar  

Some users prefer the **product switcher** in the top bar when they need to jump between Zendesk products:

- Click the **grid icon** (nine squares) → select **Guide** to enter the knowledge‑base authoring environment.  
- Choose **Chat** to open the real‑time conversation console.  

The top bar also offers a **quick‑search** shortcut: type `#12345` to jump directly to ticket 12345, regardless of which section you’re currently viewing.

### 3.3. Keyboard Shortcuts (Power‑User Tip)  

For speed, Zendesk supports a handful of keyboard shortcuts (press `?` anywhere to see the list). The most useful for navigation are:

- `g d` – Go to **Dashboard**  
- `g t` – Go to **Tickets**  
- `g v` – Open **Views** list  
- `g r` – Open **Reporting**  

Maya can practice these shortcuts during low‑traffic periods to build muscle memory.

---

## 4. Role‑Based Views: Agent vs. Admin vs. End‑User  

Zendesk tailors the interface based on the **role** assigned to a user. This is central to maintaining security and relevance.

| Role | Primary Interface Elements | What They Can See | Typical Use Cases |
|------|----------------------------|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Agent** | Sidebar (Dashboard, Tickets, Views, Reporting) | All tickets they own or are assigned to; shared views; read‑only reports. | Resolving day‑to‑day customer issues. |
| **Admin** | All Agent elements + **Admin** section (Users, Groups, Channels, Automations, etc.) | Full system configuration, all tickets, all reports, user management. | Setting up workflows, permissions, and integrations. |
| **End‑User** (Customer) | **Help Center** (public knowledge base) and **My Activities** in the portal. | Their own tickets, knowledge articles, community posts. | Submitting requests, checking status, self‑service. |

### 4.1. Visual Differences  

- **Admin** sees a gear icon (⚙️) in the sidebar, which is hidden from agents.  
- **End‑users** never see the left sidebar; instead, they navigate via the **Help Center** UI, which is a separate domain (e.g., `support.company.com`).  
- **Agents** have a **Ticket** button that displays a badge with the number of tickets awaiting their action (e.g., “5”).  

### 4.2. Permissions That Influence Navigation  

- **Ticket access** – Agents can only view tickets that belong to their **Group** or are **assigned** to them. Admins can view *all* tickets.  
- **View creation** – Only agents and admins can create Views; end‑users cannot.  
- **Reporting editing** – Only admins (or users granted the “Report Builder” permission) can edit or create new reports.  

Understanding these boundaries helps Maya avoid “permission denied” errors and know when to request assistance from an admin.

---

## 5. Personalizing the Sidebar – Faster Access to What Matters  

Zendesk allows each user to **customize** their sidebar shortcuts, turning the generic list of icons into a personalized command center.

### 5.1. Adding a Favorite View

# Chapter 3: 3. Ticket Basics: Fields, Forms, and Statuses

## A Ticket Walk‑through: From “What’s Wrong?” to “All Set”

Imagine you’ve just opened the Zendesk dashboard after a busy morning. In the **Tickets** list, a fresh entry catches your eye:

- **Subject:** *“My printer keeps jamming after the first page.”*  
- **Requester:** *Jane Doe (jane@acme.com)*  
- **Form:** *Hardware Support*  

Jane is a customer who just called the support line. She’s waiting for a solution, and you need to capture the missing details, assign the ticket to the right technician, and keep everyone (including Jane) informed about what’s happening. This single ticket will travel through a series of **fields**, **forms**, and **statuses** before it lands in the **Closed** state. Mastering each of those elements is the foundation of effective Zendesk support.

Below we break down every piece of that journey, starting with the fields that make up a ticket, moving on to custom fields and ticket forms, and finishing with the lifecycle statuses that guide agents and customers alike.

---

## 1. Standard Ticket Fields – The Core Data You’ll Always See

Zendesk tickets come with a set of **built‑in fields** that appear on every ticket, regardless of the form you use. Think of these as the “minimum résumé” a ticket must carry.

| Field | What It Holds | Why It Matters |
|-------|---------------|----------------|
| **Subject** | A concise headline of the request (often the email subject line). | Gives agents a quick glance at the issue. |
| **Description** | The full text of the request – the body of an email, chat transcript, or notes you add. | Contains the details you’ll need to troubleshoot. |
| **Requester** | The user who originated the request (email address, name, and Zendesk profile). | Identifies who to reply to and track satisfaction. |
| **Assignee** | The agent (or **group**) currently responsible for the ticket. | Makes ownership explicit and prevents duplication of effort. |
| **CC (Carbon Copy)** | Additional users who receive ticket updates – often managers or other stakeholders. | Keeps the right people in the loop without adding them as requesters. |
| **Tags** | Free‑form keywords you add (e.g., `printer`, `high_priority`). | Powerful for searching, reporting, and triggering automations later. |

> **Tip:** All of these fields are visible on the ticket view you explored in *Chapter 2 – Navigating the Zendesk Interface*. You can edit the **Subject**, type into the **Description**, and assign the ticket using the **Assignee** dropdown.

### 1.1 The Requester vs. the End‑User

In many support scenarios, the **requester** is not the same person who will ultimately use the product. For example, a corporate IT department might submit a ticket on behalf of an employee. Zendesk tracks the **requester** separately from the **assignee**, allowing you to:

- Send status updates to the requester (the person who opened the ticket).  
- Keep internal notes visible only to agents (via the **Internal Note** type).  

When you first set up your account (see *Chapter 1 – Account Setup and Initial Configuration*), you defined a **Free Trial** and later a **Paid Subscription**. Those steps gave you access to the full ticketing features, including the ability to add custom fields and forms – the next topics on our agenda.

---

## 2. Custom Ticket Fields – Capturing the Details That Matter to You

Standard fields cover the basics, but most support teams need extra data points to resolve issues efficiently. **Custom ticket fields** let you collect exactly the information you require, without cluttering the description.

### 2.1 Types of Custom Fields

| Field Type | Typical Use | Example |
|------------|-------------|---------|
| **Single‑line text** | Short, free‑form answers. | *“Serial Number”* |
| **Multi‑line text** | Longer explanations or steps taken. | *“Troubleshooting Steps Already Performed”* |
| **Dropdown (single select)** | Choose one option from a predefined list. | *“Operating System”* → Windows 10, macOS, Linux |
| **Multi‑select dropdown** | Pick multiple applicable options. | *“Affected Features”* → Printing, Scanning |
| **Numeric** | Numbers only – useful for quantities or IDs. | *“Number of Affected Devices”* |
| **Date** | Calendar dates, often for SLA calculations. | *“Installation Date”* |
| **Checkbox** | Yes/No toggle. | *“Is the device under warranty?”* |

> **Note:** Custom fields are **optional** by default. You can mark them **required** in a ticket form (see the next section) if every request of that type must include the data.

### 2.2 Adding a Custom Field – Step‑by‑Step

1. From the main navigation, click **Admin** (the gear icon) → **Ticket Fields**.  
2. Click **Add field** and select the field type you need.  
3. Fill in the **Title** (what agents will see) and **Description** (help text for requesters).  
4. Choose **Field options** where applicable (e.g., the dropdown list).  
5. Click **Save**.  

Your new field now appears on any ticket form that includes it. Remember, you can later edit or deactivate a field, but **deleting** a field permanently removes its data from all tickets – so use caution.

### 2.3 Real‑World Example: A “Device Issue” Form

Suppose your support team handles both software and hardware requests. For hardware tickets you want to capture:

- **Device Type** (dropdown: Laptop, Desktop, Printer, Router)  
- **Serial Number** (single‑line text)  
- **Warranty Status** (checkbox)  

You would create three custom fields as described above, then attach them to a **Hardware Support** ticket form (next section). When Jane submits her printer‑jamming request, the form will prompt her (or the agent on her behalf) to fill in those fields, giving the technician all the data they need before even opening the device.

---

## 3. Ticket Forms – Tailoring the Ticket Layout to the Request Type

A **ticket form** is a container that groups together the standard fields and any custom fields you’ve defined. Think of it as a **template** that appears when a ticket is created, ensuring agents collect the right data for each request category.

### 3.1 Why Use Multiple Forms?

- **Clarity:** Requesters see only the fields relevant to their issue, reducing confusion.  
- **Efficiency:** Agents receive pre‑populated data, cutting down on back‑and‑forth clarification.  
- **Automation‑Ready:** Triggers, automations, and macros can reference the form name to apply specific logic.

### 3.2 Building a Ticket Form

1. In **Admin**, go to **Ticket Forms**.  
2. Click **Add form** and give it a clear name (e.g., *“Software Bug Report”*).  
3. Drag‑and‑drop the desired **standard fields** and **custom fields** into the form layout.  
4. For each field, you can set it to **required**, **visible**, or **hidden**.  
5. Optionally, assign the form to a **group** (e.g., the *Hardware Team*) so tickets created with that form are automatically routed.  
6. Click **Save**.

> **Tip:** Keep the number of required fields low—only ask for information you truly need to start troubleshooting. Over‑asking can increase ticket‑creation friction and lead to abandoned requests.

### 3.3 Selecting the Right Form at Ticket Creation

When an end‑user submits a request via email, chat, or the **Help Center**, Zendesk automatically applies the **default form** you set in **Admin > Ticket Forms**. For more complex channels (e.g., a web form on your site), you can specify which form to use by adding a hidden field named `ticket_form_id` to the submission payload.

Agents can **change the form** after a ticket is opened if they realize the request belongs to a different category. This flexibility is handy when a request is initially mis‑routed.

### 3.4 Form‑Specific Scenario

Returning to Jane’s printer issue:

1. She clicks **Submit a request** on your Help Center and selects “Hardware Problem” from a dropdown.  
2. The Help Center loads the **Hardware Support** form, showing the custom fields *Device Type*, *Serial Number*, and *Warranty Status*.  
3. Jane fills them out, clicks **Submit**, and a new ticket appears in Zendesk with those fields already populated.  
4. The ticket is automatically assigned to the **Hardware Team** because the form is linked to that group.

Now the technician can see the serial number and warranty status at a glance, dramatically shortening the time to resolution.

## 4. Ticket Statuses – Guiding a Ticket Through Its Lifecycle

Every ticket moves through a **status** that tells both agents and requesters where the work stands. Zendesk provides five core statuses. Understanding how and when to transition between them keeps your support pipeline transparent and SLA‑friendly.

### 4.1 The Five Core Statuses

| Status | Meaning | Typical Trigger |
|--------|---------|-----------------|
| **New** | The ticket has just been created and has not yet been opened by an agent. | Automatic on ticket creation. |
| **Open** | An agent is actively working on the ticket. | Agent clicks **Open** or replies to the requester. |
| **Pending** | The ticket is waiting for external input (e.g., a customer reply, a third‑party response). | Agent selects **Pending** and adds a note explaining what’s needed. |
| **Solved** | The issue is resolved; the requester has been notified. | Agent clicks **Solve** after confirming the solution. |
| **Closed** | The ticket is archived and can no longer be reopened. | System automatically closes a **Solved** ticket after a set period (default 30 days) or an agent manually closes it. |

### 4.2 Status Transition Flow

```
New → Open → Pending ↘
                ↘   Solved → Closed
                ↗
          (Agent reopens if needed)
```

- **New → Open** – The moment an agent takes ownership or replies.  
- **Open → Pending** – When you need the requester to act (e.g., “Please provide the serial number”).  
- **Pending → Open** – Once the requester replies, you move the ticket back to **Open**.  
- **Open → Solved** – After you have confirmed the fix works.  
- **Solved → Closed** – Automatically after the configured **ticket‑closure period** or manually if you need to lock it sooner.

### 4.3 Who Can Change a Status?

- **Agents** – Can move a ticket through any status (except they cannot directly set **Closed** unless they have the *Close tickets* permission).  
- **Admins** – Have full control, including overriding any restrictions.  
- **End‑users** – Generally cannot change status, but their replies can trigger automations that move a ticket from **Pending** back to **Open**.

> **Tip:** Status changes are recorded in the ticket’s **audit log** (visible in the ticket’s timeline). This audit trail is useful for compliance and for reviewing SLA performance later.

### 4.4 Practical Walk‑through: Jane’s Ticket Journey

| Step | Action | Status Change | Reason |
|------|--------|---------------|--------|
| 1 | Jane submits the request via the Help Center. | **New** → **Open** (auto‑assigned to Hardware Team) | An agent, Alex, claims the ticket. |
| 2 | Alex asks Jane for the printer’s serial number (field already filled, but she’s unsure). | **Open** → **Pending** | Waiting for Jane’s clarification. |
| 3 | Jane replies with the serial number. | **Pending** → **Open** | Information received; work can resume. |
| 4 | Alex troubleshoots, discovers a firmware bug, and applies a fix. | **Open** → **Solved** | Issue resolved; Alex notifies Jane. |
| 5 | After 30 days with no further reply, Zendesk automatically **Closes** the ticket. | **Solved** → **Closed** | System cleanup per default closure period. |

During each transition, Zendesk automatically logs the status change and any accompanying public or internal notes, preserving a complete history of the ticket’s life.

### 4.5 Customizing Statuses (Advanced)

While the five core statuses cover most scenarios, Zendesk **Enterprise** plans allow you to add **custom statuses** (e.g., *“Escalated”*). For the purpose of this beginner guide, we’ll stick to the default set, which is sufficient for most small‑to‑mid‑size support teams.

---

## 5. Best Practices for Managing Fields, Forms, and Statuses

1. **Start Simple, Then Iterate**  
   - Begin with one ticket form per major request type.  
   - Add custom fields only when you spot a recurring data gap.

2. **Use Clear, Action‑Oriented Labels**  
   - Instead of “Device”, write “Device Type (Laptop, Printer, …)”.  
   - For statuses, rely on the default names; they are already well‑known to agents and customers.

3. **Make Required Fields Truly Required**  
   - If a field can be left blank without breaking the troubleshooting process, keep it optional.  
   - Over‑requiring fields leads to abandoned tickets or inaccurate data.

4. **Leverage Tags for Quick Filtering**  
   - Tags like `high_priority` or `needs_escalation` let you locate tickets fast, and they are later usable in triggers and reports.

5. **Document Field Purpose**  
   - Add a short description to each custom field. This description appears as placeholder/help text when agents or requesters view the form.

6. **Set Up Status‑Based SLA Policies Early**  
   - Although SLA configuration comes later (Chapter 5), aligning statuses with SLA milestones (e.g., “First response time” starts at **New**, “Resolution time” ends at **Solved**) ensures you meet expectations from day one.

7. **Regularly Review Form Usage**  
   - Periodically run a report (once you have access to reporting tools) to see which custom fields are rarely filled. Consider removing or consolidating them to keep forms lean.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Standard fields** (Subject, Description, Requester, Assignee, CC, Tags) provide the essential context for every ticket.  
- **Custom ticket fields** let you capture additional, business‑specific data; choose the appropriate field type and mark fields required only when necessary.  
- **Ticket forms** are templates that combine standard and custom fields; use separate forms for distinct request categories to streamline data entry and routing.  
- **Ticket statuses** (New → Open → Pending → Solved → Closed) map the ticket’s lifecycle; agents move tickets through these states to reflect progress and keep requesters informed.  
- Follow **best‑practice guidelines**—keep forms simple, label fields clearly, use tags wisely, and regularly audit field usage—to maintain a clean, efficient ticketing system.  

With a solid grasp of fields, forms, and statuses, you’re now equipped to design tickets that capture the right information, route them to the right people, and guide them smoothly from creation to resolution.
