# Chapter 4: 4. Users, Groups, and Permissions

## Getting the Right People on the Right Tickets  

Imagine you’re the support manager at **Luna Loom**, a fast‑growing e‑commerce brand that just launched a new line of sustainable sleepwear. Overnight, the help desk is flooded with three types of requests:  

* **Customer questions** about sizing and fabric care (end‑users).  
* **Technical tickets** from the website team about checkout errors (agents in the “Web Ops” group).  
* **Returns and refunds** that must be approved by the finance department (agents in the “Finance” group).  

If every ticket lands in a single queue, your agents will waste time sifting through unrelated issues, and sensitive financial data could be exposed to the wrong people. The solution? **Set up users, groups, and role‑based permissions in Zendesk** so each ticket automatically lands where the right people can see and resolve it.

Below you’ll learn how to:

1. **Add agents and end‑users**—both one‑by‑one and in bulk.  
2. **Organise agents into groups** that reflect skill sets or departments.  
3. **Assign roles** (admin, agent, light agent) and understand what each role can do.  
4. **Configure permission settings** to control ticket visibility and protect private data.

---

## 1. Adding People to Your Zendesk Account  

### 1.1. Manual entry – the “quick‑add” method  

When you only have a handful of new users, the fastest way is to create them directly from the Zendesk interface.

1. From the **Admin** sidebar (refer to *Navigating the Zendesk Interface*), click **People → Team**.  
2. Click **Add user** at the top‑right.  
3. Fill in the required fields:  

   * **Name** – Full name as it should appear on tickets.  
   * **Email** – Must be a valid work email; Zendesk will send an invitation.  
   * **Role** – Choose **Agent**, **Light agent**, or **Admin** (see Section 2).  

4. Click **Save**. The new user receives an email invitation to set a password and log in.

> **Tip:** If you need to add an end‑user (a customer who will submit tickets), select **End‑user** as the role. End‑users cannot log into the agent side of Zendesk but can still receive and reply to ticket notifications.

### 1.2. Bulk import – handling dozens or hundreds at once  

Most growing companies will eventually need to import many agents or customers. Zendesk provides a CSV import tool that maps columns to user attributes.

#### Step‑by‑step bulk import  

1. **Prepare the CSV file**  
   * Include a header row with exact field names: `Name, Email, Role, Group`.  
   * For agents, specify the role (`agent`, `admin`, `light_agent`).  
   * For end‑users, use `end_user`.  
   * Optional: add custom fields (e.g., `Department`) if you have them set up.  

2. **Navigate to People → Team** and click the **Import** button (usually a small arrow icon).  

3. **Upload the CSV** and review the field‑mapping screen. Zendesk will attempt to match column headings automatically; adjust any mismatches.  

4. **Run a test import** (use a small sample of 5 rows) to verify that roles and groups are assigned correctly.  

5. **Execute the full import**. Zendesk will display a progress bar and a summary report once complete.  

> **Note:** Bulk‑imported users receive the same invitation email as manually added users. If you prefer to set passwords yourself, enable the “Create users without sending invitations” option (available on paid plans).

#### Common pitfalls and how to avoid them  

| Issue | Why it happens | Fix |
|-------|----------------|-----|
| **Duplicate emails** | CSV contains the same email twice or the email already exists in Zendesk. | Remove duplicates before import or use the “Update existing users” option. |
| **Invalid role values** | Role column contains typos (`agnt` instead of `agent`). | Use the exact role strings listed in Zendesk’s documentation. |
| **Group not found** | Group name in CSV does not match any existing group. | Create the group first (see Section 2) or use the group’s numeric ID. |

## 2. Organising Agents into Groups  

### 2.1. What is a **Group**?  

A **Group** is a collection of agents who share a common responsibility—such as “Web Ops”, “Finance”, or “Customer Success”. Groups are used to:

* Route tickets automatically (via triggers, later covered in Chapter 5).  
* Control who can view or edit a ticket.  
* Generate group‑specific performance reports.

### 2.2. Creating your first groups  

1. Go to **Admin → People → Groups**.  
2. Click **Add group**.  
3. Enter a **Name** (e.g., *Web Ops*).  
4. (Optional) Add a **Description** to remind agents of the group’s purpose.  
5. Click **Save**.

Repeat the process for each department or skill set you need. For Luna Loom, you might create:

* **Customer Service** – handles general inquiries.  
* **Web Ops** – resolves technical website issues.  
* **Finance** – processes refunds and billing disputes.  
* **Product** – answers questions about materials and design.

### 2.3. Assigning agents to groups  

When adding an agent (Section 1) you can select a **Default group**. This is the group the agent belongs to by default and where tickets are initially assigned if no other routing rule applies.

* To change an agent’s group later, edit the user profile, locate the **Group** field, and select a new group.  

You can also assign an agent to **multiple groups** (available on most paid plans). In the user profile, use the **Groups** multiselect to add additional groups. This flexibility lets senior agents sit in both “Customer Service” and “Finance” if they handle escalations.

### 2.4. Using groups for ticket routing (preview)  

Although the detailed mechanics of routing are covered in Chapter 5, it helps to understand the basic principle now: **When a ticket’s “Group” field is set, only agents belonging to that group can see the ticket** (unless broader permissions are granted). This is the foundation of secure, organized support.

---

## 3. Roles: Defining What Users Can Do  

Zendesk ships with three built‑in roles. Each role bundles a set of **capabilities**—the actions a user can perform in the product. Understanding these roles is essential for both security and workflow efficiency.

| Role | Primary purpose | Key capabilities |
|------|-----------------|-------------------|
| **Admin** | Full‑access manager of the Zendesk instance. | • Create, edit, and delete users, groups, and settings.<br>• Access all tickets, including those in private groups.<br>• Manage billing, apps, and integrations. |
| **Agent** | Front‑line support staff who work tickets daily. | • View, create, edit, and solve tickets in their groups.<br>• Use macros, triggers, and automations.<br>• Access the **Help Center** for internal knowledge base articles. |
| **Light agent** | Users who need limited ticket visibility (e.g., sales reps). | • View tickets they are explicitly added to as a **CC** or **Follower**.<br>• Add private comments to tickets they can see.<br>• Cannot solve tickets or change ticket status. |

### 3.1. Assigning roles  

When adding a user (Section 1) you choose the role from a dropdown. To change a role later:

1. Open the user’s profile.  
2. Click **Edit**.  
3. Select a new role and **Save**.

> **Caution:** Only **Admins** can assign or modify the **Admin** role. If you accidentally grant admin rights to a non‑trusted user, they could change security settings or export data.

### 3.2. When to use a **Light agent**  

* **Sales teams** that need to stay informed about a customer’s support history without being able to close tickets.  
* **Subject‑matter experts** (SMEs) who provide occasional input on complex tickets but should not manage the ticket lifecycle.  

By limiting their permissions, you protect ticket integrity while still giving them the visibility they need.

### 3.3. Custom roles (advanced)  

For organizations that need a finer‑grained permission model, Zendesk offers **custom roles** on Enterprise plans. Custom roles let you toggle individual capabilities (e.g., “Can view private tickets”). Because this chapter targets beginners and core plan users, we’ll not dive into custom roles here, but keep them in mind for future scaling.

---

## 4. Controlling Ticket Access with Permissions  

### 4.1. The permission hierarchy  

Zendesk evaluates permissions in the following order (from most specific to most general):

1. **Ticket‑level restrictions** – private tickets, ticket sharing settings.  
2. **Group membership** – an agent can see tickets assigned to any of their groups.  
3. **Role capabilities** – agents can view tickets they’re allowed to see based on their role.  
4. **Organization visibility** – agents can see tickets belonging to organizations they’re linked to (if the setting is enabled).  

If any level blocks access, the agent cannot view the ticket.

### 4.2. Private vs. public tickets  

* **Public tickets** – visible to all agents (subject to group and role restrictions).  
* **Private tickets** – visible only to agents who belong to the ticket’s group and have the “View private tickets” capability (Admins have this by default).  

When creating a ticket, agents can toggle the **Private** checkbox. Private tickets are useful for:

* Sensitive financial disputes (e.g., refund amounts).  
* Internal investigations that should not be exposed to the broader support team.  

### 4.3. Configuring **Group‑based permissions**  

By default, any agent in a group can see all tickets assigned to that group. However, you can tighten control:

1. **Admin → Security → Ticket Access**.  
2. Enable **“Restrict access to tickets by group”** (available on most paid plans).  

When this option is on, agents can only view tickets that are explicitly assigned to a group they belong to. This prevents, for example, a **Customer Service** agent from accidentally opening a **Finance** ticket.

### 4.4. Organization‑level visibility  

If you have **Organizations** set up (covered in Chapter 3), you can enable **“Organization sharing”** so that all agents in the same organization can view each other’s tickets. This is handy when multiple agents need to collaborate on a single customer’s case across departments.

To toggle:

1. **Admin → People → Organizations**.  
2. Click **Settings** and turn on **“Allow agents to see tickets from other agents in the same organization.”**  

> **Best practice:** Use organization sharing sparingly. Over‑sharing can dilute the security benefits of group‑based permissions.

### 4.5. Data privacy considerations  

Zendesk stores personally identifiable information (PII) such as email addresses, phone numbers, and payment details. To stay compliant with privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA):

* **Limit who can view PII** – assign only the necessary agents (e.g., Finance) to groups that need that data.  
* **Enable data‑masking** – in **Admin → Security**, you can mask certain fields for agents with lower privileges.  
* **Audit log** – Admins can review the **Audit log** (under **Admin → Security**) to see who accessed or modified tickets containing sensitive data.

## 5. Practical Workflow: From End‑User to Resolved Ticket  

Putting the pieces together, let’s walk through a typical ticket lifecycle at **Luna Loom**.

1. **A customer submits a return request** via the web form (Ticket Basics covered earlier).  
2. The ticket is automatically **assigned to the “Finance” group** by a trigger (Chapter 5).  
3. **Finance agents** (role: **Agent**) receive the ticket in their queue. Because the ticket contains payment information, the **Private** flag is set.  
4. A **Light agent** from Sales, who is CC’d on the ticket, can view the ticket but **cannot edit** the private fields or change its status.  
5. The **Finance admin** (role: **Admin**) reviews the ticket, processes the refund, and marks the ticket **Solved**.  
6. The **Customer Service group** receives a copy of the solved ticket for future reference, but because the ticket is private, only agents with the “View private tickets” capability (Admins) can see the payment details.

Through this flow, every stakeholder sees exactly what they need—no more, no less.

The agent sees tickets from **all** of their groups. If a ticket is assigned to any of those groups, it appears in the agent’s queue.

# Chapter 5: 5. Automations, Triggers, and Macros

## Understanding Triggers vs. Automations  

When a ticket lands in Zendesk, you have two primary tools to make the system act on its own: **triggers** and **automations**. Both belong to the *Business Rules* family (see Chapter 2 for where the admin menus live), but they differ in **when** they fire and **how** they are evaluated.  

| Aspect | **Trigger** | **Automation** |
|--------|-------------|----------------|
| **Timing** | Fires **immediately** after a ticket is created or updated, as soon as the defined conditions are met. | Runs on a **schedule** (e.g., every hour, once a day). It checks tickets that already exist and meet the conditions at that moment. |
| **Typical Use** | Real‑time alerts, routing tickets to the right group, setting priorities, adding tags. | Periodic clean‑ups, SLA escalations, closing stale tickets, sending follow‑up emails. |
| **Performance Impact** | Executed for every matching event; too many complex triggers can slow ticket processing. | Executed less frequently, so they are safe for bulk operations. |
| **Visibility** | Listed under **Admin > Business Rules > Triggers**. | Listed under **Admin > Business Rules > Automations**. |

Think of a trigger as a **fire‑alarm** that rings the moment smoke appears, while an automation is a **night‑time patrol** that walks the floor every hour to spot anything that needs attention.

> **Quick tip:** Keep the number of active triggers low (under 15) and the number of automations moderate (under 10) to maintain a snappy support experience.

---

## Creating a Trigger that Notifies Agents When a High‑Priority Ticket Arrives  

### Scenario  
Your support team receives dozens of tickets each day, but **high‑priority** tickets (e.g., “System Down”) must be acted on within minutes. You want an instant, visible notification for every agent in the “Tier 1” group whenever such a ticket is created.

### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Navigate to Triggers**  
   - From any Zendesk view, click the **gear icon** (Admin) → **Business Rules** → **Triggers**.  

2. **Add a New Trigger**  
   - Click **Add trigger** (top‑right).  

3. **Name and Description**  
   - **Title:** *High‑Priority Ticket Alert*  
   - **Description (optional):** *Notifies Tier 1 agents when a ticket with priority “Urgent” is created.*  

4. **Set Conditions**  
   - **All of the following conditions must be true:**  
     - **Ticket** → **Is** → **Created** (ensures it runs only on new tickets).  
     - **Priority** → **Is** → **Urgent** (or **High**, depending on your priority naming).  
     - **Group** → **Is** → **Tier 1** (optional – limits the trigger to tickets already assigned to that group).  

5. **Define Actions**  
   - **Notify target** → **Agents in group** → **Tier 1**  
     - **Subject:** *🚨 New High‑Priority Ticket: {{ticket.id}}*  
     - **Message:**  
       ```
       A new urgent ticket has been opened.
       • Subject: {{ticket.title}}
       • Requester: {{ticket.requester.name}} ({{ticket.requester.email}})
       • Link: {{ticket.link}}
       Please respond within the SLA.
       ```  
   - **Add tag** → **high_priority_alert** (useful for reporting later).  

6. **Save**  
   - Click **Create**. The trigger is now active.

### Testing the Trigger  

1. Open a fresh ticket (use the “Submit a request” form you saw in Chapter 3).  
2. Set its **Priority** to **Urgent** and assign it to **Tier 1** (or leave unassigned if you omitted the group condition).  
3. Submit.  

All agents in the Tier 1 group should receive an email (or internal notification, depending on their notification settings) within seconds. Verify the tag **high_priority_alert** appears on the ticket.

### Common Pitfalls  

- **Over‑triggering:** If you forget the “Is Created” condition, the trigger will fire on every update, spamming agents.  
- **Missing Notification Settings:** Agents can mute email notifications; remind them to keep **Ticket Updates** turned on in their profile.  

---

## Building an Automation to Close Solved Tickets After a Set Period  

### Scenario  
Your SLA requires that tickets resolved for more than **7 days** be automatically closed to keep the queue tidy. You need a scheduled rule that identifies such tickets and transitions them to the **Closed** status without manual effort.

### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Navigate to Automations**  
   - Admin (gear) → **Business Rules** → **Automations**.  

2. **Add a New Automation**  
   - Click **Add automation**.  

3. **Name and Description**  
   - **Title:** *Auto‑Close Solved Tickets >7 Days*  
   - **Description:** *Closes tickets that have been in the “Solved” status for more than a week.*  

4. **Set Conditions**  
   - **All of the following conditions must be true:**  
     - **Ticket** → **Status** → **Is** → **Solved**  
     - **Ticket** → **Hours since solved** → **Greater than** → **168** (7 days × 24 hours).  
   - **Any of the following conditions (optional):**  
     - **Ticket** → **Group** → **Is not** → **Escalations** (exclude tickets that may need further review).  

5. **Define Actions**  
   - **Status** → **Closed**  
   - **Add tag** → **auto_closed** (helps later reporting).  

6. **Save**  

### How the Automation Works  

- The automation runs **once per hour** (Zendesk’s default schedule).  
- It scans all tickets; any ticket that meets the conditions gets its status changed to **Closed** instantly.  

### Verifying the Automation  

1. Locate a ticket that is **Solved** and has been so for more than 7 days (you can manually edit the **Solved at** date in the ticket’s **Incidents** tab if needed).  
2. Wait up to an hour, then refresh the ticket. It should now show **Closed** and carry the **auto_closed** tag.  

### Tips for Maintenance  

- **Review daily:** Go to **Automations** → **Run history** to see how many tickets were closed each run.  
- **Adjust the threshold:** If agents need more time to verify closure, change the **Hours since solved** value.  

---

## Designing and Using Macros for Common Responses  

### What Is a Macro?  

A **macro** is a predefined set of actions—typically a text response, status change, tag addition, or ticket field update—that you can apply to a ticket with a single click. Think of it as a **canned reply** that also automates routine ticket housekeeping.

### Scenario  

Your team frequently receives password‑reset requests. Instead of typing the same instructions each time, you’ll create a macro that:

1. Inserts the standard password‑reset guide.  
2. Sets the ticket status to **Pending** (awaiting user confirmation).  
3. Adds the tag **password_reset** for reporting.

### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Open the Macro Builder**  
   - Admin (gear) → **Macros** → **Add macro**.  

2. **Name the Macro**  
   - *Password Reset – Send Instructions*  

3. **Add Actions** (click **Add action** for each line):  

   - **Comment/Description** → **Public reply**  
     ```
     Hi {{ticket.requester.name}},

     To reset your password, please follow these steps:
     1. Click the “Forgot password?” link on the login page.
     2. Enter your email address and click “Submit”.
     3. Check your inbox for a reset link (it may take a few minutes).
     4. Follow the link and choose a new password.

     If you run into any issues, reply to this ticket and we’ll help you further.

     Thanks,
     {{current_user.name}}
     ```  
   - **Status** → **Pending**  
   - **Add tag** → **password_reset**  

4. **Save**  

### Applying the Macro  

1. Open any ticket that matches the scenario (e.g., subject contains “reset password”).  
2. In the ticket editor, click the **Macros** icon (lightning bolt).  
3. Select *Password Reset – Send Instructions*.  

The macro instantly inserts the formatted response, updates the status, and tags the ticket.  

### Managing Macros  

- **Organize by groups:** Use the **Group** field in the macro to limit visibility (e.g., only the **Support** group can see certain macros).  
- **Version control:** If you need to tweak wording, edit the macro and **Save as new version** to keep a history.  

### Best Practices  

- **Keep macros concise:** Long macros can overwhelm agents; break complex procedures into multiple macros if needed.  
- **Use placeholders:** `{{ticket.requester.name}}` and `{{current_user.name}}` keep messages personal.  
- **Tag consistently:** Tags like **password_reset** become powerful filters in reports (covered in Chapter 8).  

---

## Putting It All Together: A Sample End‑to‑End Workflow  

1. **Ticket Creation** – A customer submits a “System Down” request via the web form (Chapter 3).  
2. **Trigger Fires** – The *High‑Priority Ticket Alert* trigger sends an immediate notification to Tier 1 agents and tags the ticket.  
3. **Agent Response** – The agent uses the *System Down – Initial Response* macro (pre‑written with troubleshooting steps) to reply instantly, setting the ticket to **Open**.  
4. **Resolution** – After the issue is fixed, the agent marks the ticket **Solved**.  
5. **Automation Runs** – Seven days later, the *Auto‑Close Solved Tickets >7 Days* automation closes the ticket automatically, adding the **auto_closed** tag.  

This flow eliminates manual steps: the urgent alert reaches the right people instantly, the agent’s first reply is one click away, and the ticket is cleared from the queue without forgetting any stale items.

---

## Common Questions and Troubleshooting  

| Question | Answer |
|----------|--------|
| **Can a trigger and automation act on the same ticket?** | Yes. Triggers fire on creation/update; automations may later modify the ticket (e.g., close it). Just ensure they don’t conflict (e.g., an automation that re‑opens a ticket a trigger later closes). |
| **What if an agent wants to suppress a trigger notification for a specific ticket?** | Add a **checkbox custom field** called *Suppress alerts* and include it in the trigger’s conditions (`Is not` *Checked*). Agents can toggle it per ticket. |
| **Do macros work on tickets that are already closed?** | No. Closed tickets are read‑only. Use a macro that **Reopens** the ticket first, then apply the desired actions. |
| **How often do automations run?** | By default every hour. You can’t change the schedule, but you can add multiple automations with different conditions to approximate more frequent runs. |
| **Will tags added by triggers be visible in ticket reports?** | Absolutely. Tags are searchable and appear in any report that includes the **Tags** field (Chapter 8 will cover reporting). |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Triggers** act **immediately** when a ticket meets defined conditions; use them for real‑time alerts, routing, and tagging.  
- **Automations** run on a **schedule** (hourly) and are ideal for bulk actions like closing stale tickets.  
- A well‑crafted **trigger**—such as the *High‑Priority Ticket Alert*—ensures urgent issues reach the right agents instantly.  
- An **automation**—like *Auto‑Close Solved Tickets >7 Days*—keeps your ticket backlog clean without manual effort.  
- **Macros** combine canned replies with ticket updates, letting agents respond with a single click while maintaining consistency and adding useful tags.  
- Combining these tools creates streamlined, repeatable workflows that reduce response times, improve data quality, and free agents to focus on complex problems.

Imagine you’ve just launched a new feature for your SaaS product. Within the first hour, the support inbox starts filling with the same three questions: *“How do I reset my password?”*, *“Where can I find the API docs?”*, and *“Why isn’t my integration syncing?”*. Each ticket requires the same short answer, and your agents spend a disproportionate amount of time typing identical replies.  

The quickest way to stop the ticket flood is to give customers a place where they can find the answers themselves—a **Help Center** powered by Zendesk Guide. Once the Help Center is live, you can direct users to the relevant article with a single link, freeing agents to focus on more complex issues.

### 1. Turn on Guide  

1. **Navigate to the Guide admin** – From the Zendesk navigation bar (the one you explored in *Navigating the Zendesk Interface*), click the **Products** menu and select **Guide**.  
2. **Start the setup wizard** – If Guide is still disabled, you’ll see a banner prompting you to **Enable Guide**. Click **Get started**.

4. **Confirm the subdomain** – The subdomain you selected during *Account Setup* (e.g., `yourcompany.zendesk.com`) will also serve as the URL for the Help Center (`support.yourcompany.com` if you set up a custom domain).  

> **Tip:** The Help Center lives on the same Zendesk instance as your tickets, so all the **Users**, **Groups**, and **Permissions** you defined earlier are instantly available for controlling article access.

### 2. Select a Theme  

A **theme** is the visual template that determines colors, fonts, layout, and responsive behavior of your Help Center. Zendesk ships with several pre‑built themes:

| Theme | When to use it |
|-------|----------------|
| **Classic** | Simple, clean look; good for minimal branding. |
| **Modern** | Bold colors, larger hero images; fits startups that want a splashy front page. |
| **Help Center Starter** | Designed for quick launch; includes ready‑made sections for common support topics. |

1. In Guide, go to **Guide admin > Customize design**.  
2. Click **Change theme** and preview each option.  
3. Select the theme that matches your brand style and click **Apply**.  

If you prefer a completely custom look, the **Theme editor** lets you edit HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. For beginners, we recommend sticking with a built‑in theme and tweaking colors via the **Branding** panel (logo, primary color, accent color).

## Writing and Organizing Articles  

A Help Center is only as useful as its content. The goal is to create **self‑service resources** that are easy to find and understand. Below is a step‑by‑step workflow that mirrors the way you’d create a ticket in Zendesk, but with a focus on knowledge sharing instead of problem resolution.

### 1. Create the First Article  

1. **Open the article editor** – In Guide admin, click **Add article** (top‑right).  
2. **Title** – Use a clear, searchable phrase. *“How to reset your password”* is better than *“Password help”*.  
3. **Body** – The rich‑text editor lets you add headings, lists, images, and videos.  
   - **Use headings** (`<h2>`, `<h3>`) to break steps into logical chunks.  
   - **Add screenshots** by dragging them into the editor; Zendesk automatically hosts the image.  
   - **Include a “Related articles”** section at the bottom to guide users to other relevant content.  
4. **Save as draft** – This keeps the article invisible to the public until you’re ready.  

> **Note:** Because you already know how to **add attachments** to tickets (see *Ticket Basics*), you’ll find the same process here when inserting images.

### 2. Build the Hierarchical Structure  

Zendesk Guide organizes content in a three‑level hierarchy:

1. **Categories** – Top‑level containers (e.g., *Getting Started*, *Account Management*, *Technical Issues*).  
2. **Sections** – Sub‑folders within a category (e.g., under *Technical Issues*: *API*, *Integrations*, *Troubleshooting*).  
3. **Articles** – Individual knowledge pieces.

#### Best‑practice steps  

1. **Sketch a map** – Before you click “Add category,” sketch a quick outline on paper or a whiteboard.  
2. **Create categories** – In Guide admin, click **Add category**. Keep the number to 4‑6; too many top‑level items overwhelm visitors.  
3. **Add sections** – Inside each category, click **Add section**. Aim for 2‑4 sections per category.  
4. **Place articles** – Drag and drop articles into the appropriate section, or select the section while creating the article.  

**Example hierarchy for a SaaS startup**

```
Getting Started
 └─ Account Setup
     ├─ How to create an account
     └─ How to verify your email
Technical Issues
 └─ API
     ├─ Authentication guide
     └─ Rate‑limit FAQ
```

### 3. Writing Tips for Beginners  

- **Answer the “What, Why, How”** in the first paragraph.  
- **Use plain language** – Avoid internal jargon unless you define it.  
- **Keep steps short** – One action per bullet.  
- **Add a “Last updated” date** – Shows the article is maintained.  

---

## Setting Up Article Permissions  

Not every article should be visible to every visitor. Zendesk Guide respects the same **Roles** and **Groups** you configured in *Users, Groups, and Permissions*.

### 1. Permission Levels  

| Permission | Who can see it |
|------------|----------------|
| **Public** | Anyone on the internet (default). |
| **Signed‑in** | Only logged‑in users (any role). |
| **Internal** | Agents only; useful for troubleshooting guides. |
| **Restricted** | Specific groups or organizations (e.g., premium customers). |

### 2. Applying Permissions  

1. Open an article in edit mode.  
2. Click the **Permissions** tab.  
3. Choose one of the four options.  
4. If you select **Restricted**, a dropdown appears where you can pick the groups that have access.  

> **Tip:** Use **Internal** articles for “How to troubleshoot a failed webhook” – this prevents customers from seeing internal processes while still giving agents a quick reference.

### 3. Controlling Access at the Section Level  

Permissions can also be set at the **section** level, cascading down to all articles within. This is handy when you have an entire category meant for **Partner** users only.  

---

## Optimizing Articles for Search Engines (SEO)  

Even the best‑written article is useless if users can’t find it. Zendesk Guide offers built‑in SEO controls that let you influence how search engines rank your pages.

### 1. Edit SEO Settings  

1. While editing an article, click the **SEO** tab.  
2. Fill in the following fields:  

   - **Meta title** – Usually the article title plus your brand (e.g., “Reset your password – Acme Support”).  
   - **Meta description** – A concise 150‑160‑character summary; appears under the title in Google results.  
   - **Slug** – The URL part after the domain (e.g., `reset-password`). Keep it short and keyword‑rich.  

### 2. Keywords and Internal Search  

- **Keyword focus** – Identify the primary phrase users will type (e.g., “reset password”). Use it naturally in the title, headings, and first paragraph.  
- **Internal search** – Guide’s built‑in search uses the same content. Adding **tags** (via the **Add tag** field) helps surface articles when customers type related terms.  

### 3. Robots and Indexing  

For **Internal** or **Restricted** articles, Zendesk automatically adds a `noindex` meta tag, preventing search engines from crawling them. For public articles, you can control indexing by toggling the **Allow search engines to index this article** switch.

# Chapter 7: 7. Multichannel Support: Email, Chat, Phone, and Social

## Why Multichannel Matters  

Imagine Maya, a customer‑service manager at a fast‑growing e‑commerce brand. Over a single weekend her team receives **200 emails**, **120 live‑chat requests**, **30 phone calls**, and a flurry of **Twitter mentions**. Each channel lives in a different inbox, phone system, or social‑media dashboard, and agents spend precious minutes switching between tools, often missing or duplicating tickets.  

When Maya consolidates every inbound request into **Zendesk**, her agents see **one unified ticket list**, can apply the same **triggers** and **macros** they already use for email, and route each conversation to the right group with a single click. The result? Faster response times, happier customers, and a clearer view of support workload.  

In this chapter you’ll learn how to **connect each support channel**—email, chat, phone, and social—so that all interactions flow into Zendesk tickets you already know how to manage.

## Setting Up Email Support  

### 1. Choose Your Email Strategy  

| Option | How it works | When it’s best |
|--------|--------------|----------------|
| **Zendesk‑provided address** (e.g., support@yourcompany.zendesk.com) | Zendesk automatically creates tickets from incoming mail. No forwarding needed. | Small teams, quick start, no custom domain. |
| **Custom support address** (e.g., support@yourcompany.com) | Your existing mailbox forwards messages to Zendesk. Gives brand consistency. | Established brands that already own a support address. |

### 2. Connect a Custom Support Email  

1. **Navigate to** **Admin ▶ Channels ▶ Email**.  
2. Click **Add address** and enter the full email you want Zendesk to monitor (e.g., **support@yourcompany.com**).  
3. Zendesk will display **MX record** and **SPF** values. Add these to your domain’s DNS so mail servers trust Zendesk as a legitimate sender.  
4. Click **Verify**. Once the DNS changes propagate (usually < 24 h), Zendesk will show a green checkmark.

> **Tip:** If you’re unsure how to edit DNS records, your domain registrar’s help center usually has step‑by‑step guides.  

### 3. Set Up Forwarding Rules (if you keep the mailbox in Gmail, Outlook, etc.)  

| Platform | Forwarding steps |
|----------|-----------------|
| **Gmail** | *Settings ▶ Forwarding and POP/IMAP* → **Add a forwarding address** → enter the **Zendesk‑generated address** shown in the previous step → confirm the verification email. |
| **Outlook/Office 365** | *Admin Center ▶ Exchange* → **Mail flow** → **Rules** → **+ Add a rule** → **Apply to all messages** → **Redirect the message to** → paste the Zendesk address. |
| **Other providers** | Look for “Auto‑forward” or “Mail Forwarding” in the admin console and point to the Zendesk address. |

> **Tip:** Add a **subject prefix** (e.g., `[Support]`) in the forwarding rule. This makes it easier to create triggers later that only fire on support‑related mail.

### 4. Test the Connection  

Send a test email from a personal address to the support address. Within a few seconds you should see a **new ticket** appear in Zendesk under **Tickets ▶ All**. Open the ticket and verify:

* **Subject** matches the email.
* **Requester** is the sender’s address.

## 5. Understanding SLA Metrics  

### 5.1 What is an SLA?  

**SLA (Service Level Agreement)** is a contract‑like promise that defines how quickly your support team must respond to or resolve a ticket. Common SLA targets include:

- **First Reply** – Time from ticket creation to the first public reply.  
- **Resolution** – Time from creation to ticket status “Solved”.  
- **Urgent Ticket** – Faster response for high‑priority tickets.

Zendesk stores SLA definitions under **Admin → Business Rules → SLAs**.

### 5.2 Where SLA data lives in reports  

When you add an **“SLA compliance”** widget to a dashboard, Zendesk automatically calculates:

- **% of tickets meeting the SLA** (e.g., 92% of first‑reply SLA met).  
- **Average breach time** (how long after the deadline tickets remained open).  

These metrics appear as **kpi cards** (large numbers) and as **trend graphs** over selected periods.

## Start with a Ticket Audit: Find the Hidden Slowdowns

A ticket audit is a review of recent tickets to spot patterns, delays, or inefficiencies in your workflow. Think of it as a health check for your support process.

### How to Run a Basic Ticket Audit

1. **Pick a time range** – Start with the last 7–30 days. Too short, and you won’t see patterns. Too long, and the data may not reflect current processes.
2. **Filter tickets by status** – Focus on **open**, **pending**, and **solved** tickets. These reveal where work is piling up.
3. **Look for these red flags:**
   - **Tickets stuck in one status too long** – e.g., “pending” for more than 24 hours.
   - **Frequent reassignments** – a ticket moved between groups or agents multiple times.
   - **Long resolution times** – compare average time to industry benchmarks if you have them.
4. **Group by agent or channel** – Is one agent consistently slower? Are chat tickets resolved faster than email?

> **Tip:** Use Zendesk’s built-in filters and views to create a custom “Audit View.” Save it so you can reuse it each month.

For example, Luna Loom might find that **30% of tickets** are being reassigned because the wrong group was assigned initially. That points to a training or routing issue—not a people problem.

---

## Build Feedback Loops: Use Surveys to Guide Improvements

Customer feedback is your compass. Zendesk’s **satisfaction surveys** (CSAT) give direct input from users on every ticket. But it’s not enough to collect the data—you need to act on it.

### How to Set Up and Use CSAT Surveys

1. **Enable CSAT in Admin Settings** → **Customer Satisfaction** → Turn on “Allow customers to rate this ticket.”
2. **Choose when to send the survey** – After the ticket is solved, or after every reply.
3. **Review results regularly** – Check the **CSAT report** in Zendesk Analytics (from Chapter 8).
4. **Look for patterns:**
   - Low scores on specific ticket types (e.g., refunds, cancellations).
   - Repeated negative comments about a particular agent.
   - High scores on certain knowledge base articles.

> **Tip:** Add a custom survey question: “What could we have done better?” This gives qualitative insight.

Luna Loom noticed that **42% of low CSAT scores** were linked to slow responses on weekend tickets. They realized their weekend coverage was inconsistent. By adjusting agent schedules and setting weekend SLAs, they improved satisfaction by 22% in one month.

---

## Keep Your Knowledge Base Clean: A Living Resource

A stale knowledge base is worse than no knowledge base. Articles that are outdated, hard to find, or incorrect erode trust and increase ticket volume.

### How to Maintain Knowledge Base Hygiene

1. **Assign ownership** – One person (or team) should be responsible for reviewing articles each quarter.
2. **Create a review checklist:**
   - Is the information still accurate?
   - Are links working?
   - Does the article match current product or policy changes?
   - Is it easy to understand for beginners?
3. **Use article labels and categories** – Helps agents and customers find relevant info faster.
4. **Retire old articles** – Don’t just delete—redirect users to updated versions when possible.
5. **Track usage data** – Check which articles are viewed most (and least). High views but low resolution? That article might need improvement.

> **Tip:** Schedule a “knowledge base cleanup day” every quarter. Block 2–4 hours to review and update.

Luna Loom found an article on “How to return a product” that still referenced their old return address. After updating it, ticket volume on returns dropped by 15%.

---

## Review Automations, Triggers, and Macros Quarterly

Automations, triggers, and macros are powerful—but they can become outdated or redundant over time. A monthly coupon code trigger from a past promotion might still be firing, clogging your system with irrelevant tickets.

### How to Audit Your Automation Stack

1. **List all active automations, triggers, and macros.**
   - In Admin → **Objects and rules** → Automations, Triggers, Macros.
2. **Check for these issues:**
   - **Orphaned rules** – Rules that no longer apply (e.g., expired promotions).
   - **Overlapping rules** – Two triggers doing the same thing, causing confusion.
   - **Unused macros** – Macros created but never applied.
3. **Test each rule** – Change one variable in a test ticket to confirm it triggers as expected.
4. **Document changes** – Keep a simple log of what you change and why.

> **Tip:** Use meaningful names for rules—e.g., “Auto-assign Tier 2: Billing Issues” instead of “Trigger 7.”

### **A. Automations**
- **Purpose**: Time-based actions (e.g., "After 24 hours, escalate ticket").
- **Triggers**:
  - **Conditions**: Ticket field values (e.g., "Priority = High").
  - **Actions**: Assign to group, notify agent, change status.
- **Examples**:

### **B. Triggers**
- **Event-Based Automation**: Runs when a ticket is created or updated.
- **Use Cases**:
  - Send an auto-response when a ticket is submitted.
  - Tag tickets based on subject keywords (e.g., "Refund").
- **Conditions vs. Actions**:
  - **Conditions**: "If ticket priority is Urgent."
  - **Actions**: "Notify admin, set status to Open."

### **C. Macros**
- **Purpose**: Pre-written responses or actions to standardize replies.
- **Types**:
  - **Ticket Macros**: Apply to a single ticket (e.g., "Thanks for contacting us!").
  - **Bulk Macros**: Apply to multiple tickets (e.g., "Mark as solved").
- **Dynamic Content**: Personalize macros with placeholders (e.g., `{{ticket.subject}}`).
- **Examples**:

  - A "Password Reset" macro with step-by-step instructions.

### **Glossary: Zendesk Customer Support Terms**

1. **Ticket**
   A single customer issue or request, tracked in Zendesk as a record of communication. Tickets contain conversations, attachments, and metadata (e.g., priority, status).

2. **Support Request**
   A customer’s initial inquiry (e.g., email, chat, or form submission) that generates a ticket in Zendesk. It may include details like user info, category, or urgency.

3. **Agent**
   A Zendesk user (employee) who responds to tickets, resolves issues, and interacts with customers. Agents can be assigned roles (e.g., support, admin, or manager).

4. **Trigger**
   An automated workflow that performs actions (e.g., sending emails, updating fields) based on ticket conditions (e.g., "If priority = high, assign to Tier 2 team").

5. **Macro**
   Pre-saved responses or actions (e.g., canned replies, status updates) that agents can apply to tickets to save time. Macros can be personalized or organization-wide.

6. **View**
   A filtered list of tickets based on criteria (e.g., "Unassigned," "High Priority," or "Created in the last 24 hours"). Views help agents prioritize work.

7. **SLA (Service Level Agreement)**
   A policy defining response/resolution timeframes (e.g., "First reply within 2 hours for high-priority tickets"). Zendesk tracks SLA compliance in dashboards.

8. **Channel**
   The medium through which customers submit tickets (e.g., email, live chat, phone, social media, or web forms). Zendesk supports omnichannel routing.

9. **Automation**
   Rules that streamline repetitive tasks (e.g., auto-assigning tickets, closing resolved requests, or notifying customers). Automations reduce manual work.

10. **App (or Zendesk App)**
    Third-party integrations (e.g., Slack, Salesforce, or payment tools) that extend Zendesk’s functionality. Apps can be installed via the Zendesk Marketplace.

11. **Knowledge Base (Help Center)**
    A self-service repository of articles, FAQs, and guides that empower customers to resolve issues independently. Integrated with Zendesk for easy access.

12. **Collaborator**
    An external user (e.g., vendor or colleague) who can view or comment on a ticket without full agent access. Useful for cross-team collaboration.

13. **Organization**
    A group of end-users (customers) who share a Zendesk account. Organizations help manage permissions, SLAs, and reporting by segmenting users.

14. **Report**
    Data-driven insights (e.g., ticket volume, resolution time, agent performance) generated in Zendesk’s reporting tools. Helps track support efficiency.

15. **Explore (Zendesk Explore)**
    Zendesk’s native analytics tool that visualizes support metrics (e.g., CSAT scores, ticket trends) in dashboards and reports. Requires data export from tickets.
